title: CoraxReads cloud architecture comparisons
text: CoraxReads cloud architecture comparisons AWS is the course's primary cloud path. These three diagrams show equivalent conceptual production-style building blocks so learners can recognize the pattern across providers. They are not deployment instructions, do not create cloud resources, and do not replace the course's smaller Week 9 exercise or instructor approval. AWS primary: Route 53 provides DNS, an Application Load Balancer routes HTTPS traffic, ECS runs the app, RDS stores relational data, and CloudWatch collects operational signals. IAM task roles grant the service only the access it needs. Actual networking, certificates, backups, redundancy, and pricing require a design review. Azure comparison: Azure DNS, Application Gateway, App Service, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Monitor, and managed identities fill similar roles. Names and capabilities differ; this diagram is a mapping aid, not a claim that the services are identical. Google Cloud comparison: Cloud DNS, an external Application Load Balancer, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Cloud Monitoring/Logging, and a service account are analogous building blocks. Verify regional availability, network paths, and current service/pricing details before any real design. Safe learning sequence 1. Draw and explain the local browser → Express API → PostgreSQL flow first. 2. Compare the three diagrams and label each service by role, not just by vendor name. 3. Keep the course's Week 6–8 practice local. Week 9 uses AWS only, after the instructor approves the cost limit, account protections, and teardown steps. 4. Do not create Azure or Google Cloud accounts for this comparison exercise. 5. Before any real cloud deployment, add TLS, private database networking, secrets management, least-privilege identity, backups, monitoring, budget alerts, and a tested cleanup plan. Budget alerts are not hard spending caps.

title: Learner Portfolio Guide
text: Learner Portfolio Guide Your course repo is the lesson book. Your portfolio repo is your own work. Do not edit the course files to submit assignments. Suggested portfolio layout Create folders as you reach each week. Keep notes, diagrams, scripts, test evidence, and runbooks in the matching week folder. Avoid committing screenshots that reveal personal details. Weekly submission checklist For each assignment: 1. Read the overview and all three class guides. 2. Read the assignment once before running commands. 3. Check the where to run commands instructions. 4. Copy commands carefully; replace example names/ports only when the guide says to. 5. After each step, compare your output with the expected result. 6. If it differs, stop and use the week's troubleshooting guide before trying random fixes. 7. Save a short reflection: what worked, what broke, how you verified the repair. 8. Review git status and git diff before committing. 9. Remove secrets and personal information before pushing. 10. Submit the portfolio link and any requested pull-request or demo link. Explain commands in plain words Use this pattern in your notes: Do not submit a command list without explaining why the command is safe and relevant. Protect your work - Never commit .env, passwords, API keys, access tokens, private keys, or cloud credentials. - A private repository is not a secret manager. - Use a display name and blur usernames, account IDs, email addresses, private IPs, browser tabs, and billing details if you do not want them public. - If you accidentally publish a credential, treat it as compromised: revoke/rotate it and tell the account owner. Deleting the line is not enough. - Never run destructive commands on a shared or production environment. Official documentation Each week's overview links to official documentation. Use it to confirm current tool behavior and versions; the course examples are practice starting points, not substitutes for current vendor guidance.

title: CoraxShift DevOps Academy
text: CoraxShift DevOps Academy Learn by building. Break it. Fix it. Ship it. 12-week roadmap 3 classes / week 2 hours / class 1 learning project 12 badges Course status: All 12 weeks have an overview, three class guides, a practical assignment, troubleshooting notes, and a weekly quiz. A local-first learning portal and CoraxReads teaching app make it easier to explore and practice the course. See the full curriculum for the week-by-week roadmap. New learners should also read the portfolio submission guide. Preview the CoraxShift learning portal, browse the curated open-source project references, and compare the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud architecture diagrams. What is CoraxShift? CoraxShift is a portfolio-based DevOps academy. You do not just watch. You build, you break, you fix, you ship. One project from Week 1 to Week 12. One portfolio that proves what you can do. Who is this for? - Beginners with no tech background - Career changers who want proof, not just certificates - Students who want to explain what they built in plain words - Anyone who wants to learn DevOps by doing, not by memorizing No experience needed. We start from zero and explain every command. What you will build CoraxReads - a sample bookstore project used to learn DevOps one step at a time. - Week 1: Understand how a browser finds and talks to a website - Week 2: Serve a simple practice page with Nginx in a Codespace - Weeks 3-8: Learn scripting, Git, delivery planning, Terraform, Ansible, and Docker - Week 9: Learn the cloud using one AWS account and a billing alert - Weeks 10-12: Learn Kubernetes, monitoring, CI/CD, and present the capstone Your portfolio starts in Week 1. Every week you push. How it works - 3 classes per week, 2 hours each - Every class: Where to run commands, what each command does, expected output, what you should see after - Every week: Hands-on project, push to portfolio, pass checklist - Every week: Quiz at end of Class 3, 12 questions, 20 minutes - Every week: 90 percent earns the weekly badge 12-Week Curriculum Week Focus What you ship --- --- --- 1. Essentials Internet, networking, tools Internet diagram, workstation check, project explanation 2. Linux Linux, Nginx, operations Local practice page, health-check script, maintenance notes 3. Bash Shell automation Health check and verified backup scripts 4. Git GitHub collaboration Reviewed pull request and conflict-resolution evidence 5. SDLC Plan, test, release Feature issue, test plan, release and rollback notes 6. Terraform Infrastructure as code Local Docker infrastructure, reviewed plan, cleanup proof 7. Ansible Configuration automation Repeatable Nginx playbook and idempotency evidence 8. Docker Containers and Compose App + database stack with persistent data 9. AWS Cloud foundations Cost guardrails, small approved deployment, teardown 10. Kubernetes Local orchestration Local cluster, workload, Service, probes, runbook 11. CI/CD + observability Delivery and operations CI workflow, dashboard, alert, recovery notes 12. Capstone Integration and presentation Demonstrable system, documentation, recovery, reflection How the project fits together We start with a simple page, then add the parts a real application needs. Think of it like a bookstore: the page is the shop window, the backend is the clerk handling requests, and the database is the stock ledger. In Week 2, the practice page is served by Nginx on your Codespace. That is a local learning exercise, not the finished cloud architecture. The response travels back along the same path to the browser. Quiz and Badge - Quiz: Per week, not per class. 12 questions per week: 8 single-answer, 4 multiple-answer - Style: Technical, not ABC. Scenario, output, and fix based, from that week's lab - Pass: 11 out of 12, 90 percent, earns the weekly badge - If below 90 percent: Review, retake once - Total: 12 badges. Each badge goes in your portfolio README What you need - A laptop - A GitHub account - 5 to 7 hours per week - Codespaces as a practice environment until Week 9 No cloud account until Week 9. In Weeks 6 to 8, practice Terraform, Ansible, and Docker locally. In Week 9, use one AWS account, set a billing alert before creating resources, and remove resources when you finish. Week 10 uses local Kubernetes. AWS billing alerts are not spending caps, so follow the cleanup checklist and review current pricing. Example stack for CoraxReads - Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript - Backend: Node.js + Express - Database: PostgreSQL What we promise We promise skills and proof. A portfolio you can show, a demo you can explain, and badges you earned by passing technical quizzes. We do not promise a job. No academy can promise that. What we promise is that you will finish with work you can defend in an interview. How to start 1. Open this private repo in Codespaces and preview the learning portal. 2. Open the Week 1 overview. 3. Start Class 1, do the lab, and push your work to your separate portfolio repo. 4. Share your Week 1 assignment only after checking it contains no credentials or private course material. The lessons live here. Your own exercises, screenshots, and portfolio work belong in your separate portfolio repository. Never put passwords, API keys, or cloud credentials in either repository. For students This repo is private because students pay for it. Your portfolio repo is public. That is where you show your work. Build. Break. Fix. Ship. Welcome to CoraxShift.

title: CoraxShift Curriculum - 12 Weeks, One Real Project
text: CoraxShift Curriculum - 12 Weeks, One Real Project Project: CoraxReads, a sample bookstore app used throughout the course. You learn the pieces in stages and present your capstone in Week 12. This is the complete course roadmap. Every week has an overview, three class guides, a practical assignment, troubleshooting notes, and a weekly quiz. Later-week activities are educational labs; they are not production infrastructure. Start with the Week 1 overview or Week 2 overview, then follow the weekly links in the README. Use the local learning portal to search lesson topics and take interactive quizzes. The quiz answers and explanations are read from the same weekly Markdown files used in the course. Optional project references for each week are listed in the open-source project guide; compare the AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud diagrams without creating extra cloud accounts. The project in one picture The analogy is only a way to remember the roles: the backend validates requests and applies rules; the database stores the bookstore's data. Week 1: Essentials - Internet, Networking and Tools Basics Learn: What happens when you type a website. DNS, IP, port, HTTP, TCP, and what a server does. Build: Set up VS Code and a terminal. Draw how a request travels from browser to server. Install later-week tools only when a lesson needs them. Push: Your diagram + tool check list + project idea doc for CoraxReads. Week 2: Linux for DevOps Learn: Files, permissions, users, processes, logs, basic networking commands. How to read a log and find the problem. Build: Serve a simple CoraxReads practice page with Nginx in a Codespace. Manage it with commands, check logs, and learn safe file permissions. Push: Screenshots of your commands + a short log troubleshooting note. Week 3: Bash for DevOps Learn: Bash in plain words. Variables, if, loops, functions. How to automate boring work. Build: Write a healthcheck script and a dated backup script for your project. Learn why safe automation validates inputs and never deletes unknown paths. Push: Your scripts + how to run them + proof the backup can be restored. Week 4: Git and GitHub Learn: Git workflow a real team uses. Branch, commit, merge, pull request, review, conflict. Build: Put CoraxReads in Git properly. Create a dev branch, open a PR, fix a practice merge conflict, write a clean commit history. Push: A clean repo with branches, PRs, and a good README. Week 5: SDLC Learn: SDLC from idea to production. Plan, build, test, release, monitor. Where DevOps sits in it. Build: Write the SDLC for CoraxReads. User stories, test plan, release plan, rollback plan. Push: Your SDLC doc + release checklist. Week 6: Terraform Learn: Infrastructure as Code. Provider, resource, state, variables, plan and apply. No cloud yet. Build: Write Terraform that builds practice infrastructure locally with Docker. You learn the workflow without touching a cloud account. Push: Your Terraform files + a note on what plan and apply did. Week 7: Ansible Learn: Configuration as Code. Inventory, playbook, task, role. How to set up a server the same way every time. Build: Write an Ansible playbook that sets up a fresh practice server: installs Docker, copies your app, and starts it. Push: Your playbook + proof it ran on a fresh target. Week 8: Docker Learn: Image, container, Dockerfile, volume, network, Compose. Why Docker fixes it works on my machine. Build: Write a Dockerfile for CoraxReads. Run it with Compose with the app + PostgreSQL database. Push: Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and how to run it. Week 9: AWS Cloud Week Learn: Cloud computing in plain words: compute, storage, networking, and IAM. Learn what billing alerts do and why free-tier use can still cost money. Build: Create ONE AWS account only. Set a billing alert before creating resources. Deploy a small CoraxReads practice page to an approved VM. Other cloud providers are comparison topics only; do not create extra accounts for this course. Push: Your cloud setup doc + billing alert screenshot + your live app link + cost notes. Stop the server when you are done. Week 10: Kubernetes Learn: Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, scaling. Why teams use Kubernetes. Build: Deploy CoraxReads to Kubernetes. First on kind locally, then to your AWS practice environment. Add a Service, Ingress, and scaling. Push: Your Kubernetes manifests + how to check pods, services, and logs. Week 11: Capstone Part 1 - Full Pipeline Learn: How the pieces connect. A reviewed change triggers CI, CI tests and builds Docker, and an approved deployment updates the practice environment. Build: Connect your pipeline end to end. A reviewed merge starts deployment, a health check confirms success, and a documented rollback restores the previous version if needed. Push: Your pipeline file + a run log that shows it worked. Week 12: Capstone Part 2 - Demo, Docs, Portfolio Learn: How to present your work like a professional. Build: Add monitoring, clean docs, architecture diagram, demo video, and portfolio README. Clean up cloud resources so you do not get charged. Push: Final capstone repo + demo + portfolio README. This is what you show employers.

title: Assignment 1: Basic Understanding of Internet, Networking and Tools Basics
text: Assignment 1: Basic Understanding of Internet, Networking and Tools Basics Time: 120 to 180 minutes Level: Beginner Submit in: Your portfolio repo, in folder modules/01-essentials/assignment-1 Overview You are starting your DevOps journey. You will prove you understand the foundations by explaining them, drawing them, and showing evidence from your own computer. Scenario You are supporting CoraxReads, a small online bookstore built by CoraxShift. It is hosted in Lagos. A user in the USA wants to open it. Your job is to explain how that works, compare architectures, fix the DNS, set up your tools, and share what you learned. Learning Outcomes By the end, you will be able to: 1. Use ChatGPT as a learning assistant, with a clear prompt 2. Explain how internet communication works across countries 3. Explain packet switching, IP address, TCP/IP, and HTTP/HTTPS in your own words 4. Compare two-tier and three-tier architecture with original diagrams 5. Explain DNS and pick the right record for an IPv4 address 6. Set up VS Code and verify it with your own terminal 7. Share your learning in a clear LinkedIn post Rules 1. Write in your own words. Do not copy ChatGPT output as your answer. 2. All diagrams must be yours. Hand drawn or draw.io, both are fine. 3. Use your own computer for screenshots. You may blur your username and other personal details before sharing them. 4. Do not paste passwords, tokens, or keys in any screenshot. 5. Keep Tasks 1 to 6 in order, in one folder, with clear headings. What you need Internet, a Google account for LinkedIn, a browser, VS Code, ChatGPT free account. Task 1 - Use ChatGPT as Your Learning Assistant Goal: Write a clear prompt and learn one concept well. Steps: 1. Open ChatGPT 2. Write a prompt like this, in your own words: Explain TCP/IP to a beginner. Use beginner-friendly language and one real-life example, like sending a letter or making a phone call. 3. Read the answer. Check that it has a simple definition and a real-life example. 4. Take a screenshot of your prompt and the answer. What to submit: Screenshot 1 - Your ChatGPT prompt and answer. Task 2 - Internet and Networking Scenario: Your friend runs CoraxReads in Lagos. A user in the USA wants to open it. Goal: Explain in 100 to 150 words how that user in the USA can open a website hosted in Lagos. Your explanation must clearly cover, in your own words: Packet switching, IP address, TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS What to submit: Your 100 to 150 word explanation, under Task 2 heading. No screenshot needed. Task 3 - Application Architecture and Stack Scenario: CoraxReads has two versions. Two-tier: Frontend and Database. Three-tier: Frontend, Backend, and Database. Goal: Compare them with original diagrams. Steps: 1. Draw a two-tier diagram. Show Frontend and Database. Label every layer. Show arrows for communication. 2. Draw a three-tier diagram. Show Frontend, Backend, and Database. Label every layer. Show arrows. 3. For Frontend, list at least 2 technologies. Example: HTML, React. 4. For Backend, list at least 2 technologies. Example: Node.js, Python. 5. For Database, list at least 2 technologies. Example: PostgreSQL, MongoDB. What to submit: Screenshot 2 - Your two diagrams, with labels visible. Task 4 - Domain Name and DNS Scenario: CoraxReads can be opened today by IP 102.130.45.78 at port 3000. Your friend bought the domain coraxreads.com. Goal: Explain DNS and pick the right record. Steps: 1. In 50 to 100 words, in your own words, explain what DNS is. 2. Say which DNS record your friend should use to connect coraxreads.com to 102.130.45.78, and why. 3. Keep it conceptual. You do not need to configure DNS in this task. What to submit: Your 50 to 100 word explanation plus your record answer. Note: DNS maps the domain to the IP. Port 3000 is handled separately by the app or web server, not by DNS. Task 5 - VS Code Setup, Hands-On Goal: Set up VS Code and prove it is yours. Steps: 1. Install VS Code if you do not have it. 2. Open VS Code. Pick a theme you like. 3. Open the integrated terminal: Terminal menu, then New Terminal. 4. Run a command for your system: If you use Windows: whoami, then dir If you use Mac or Linux: whoami, then pwd, then ls 5. Take a screenshot showing VS Code, your theme, and your terminal. Blur your username if you do not want it public. What to submit: Screenshot 3 - Your VS Code window with theme and terminal output. Blur your username if you do not want it public. Task 6 - Publish Your Learning as a LinkedIn Post Goal: Summarize Tasks 1 to 5 in public, in your own words. Steps: 1. Write a LinkedIn post with clear sections: ChatGPT, Internet and Networking, Architecture, DNS, VS Code Setup. 2. Write it in your own words. Add 1 or 2 screenshots from your assignment. 3. Add this credit note exactly at the end: P.S. This post is part of CoraxShift DevOps Academy - Week 1. Learn by building: https://github.com/coraxshift-academy 4. Publish it so reviewers can see it. 5. Copy the LinkedIn URL into your assignment folder. 6. Take a screenshot of the published post. What to submit: Screenshot 4 - Published LinkedIn post plus the LinkedIn URL. Submission Checklist - Tasks 1 to 6 in order, in your portfolio folder - Screenshot 1: ChatGPT prompt and answer - Task 2: 100 to 150 word explanation, with packet switching, IP, TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS - Screenshot 2: Two-tier and three-tier diagrams, labelled, with tech examples - Task 4: 50 to 100 word DNS explanation plus correct record - Screenshot 3: VS Code with theme, terminal, your username - Screenshot 4: LinkedIn post plus URL plus CoraxShift credit note - No passwords, keys, tokens, or personal information you do not want to publish - All writing in your own words Final Submission Submit your portfolio folder link for modules/01-essentials/assignment-1 plus your LinkedIn post URL.

title: Class 1: Internet, Networking, Domain and DNS
text: Class 1: Internet, Networking, Domain and DNS Time: 2 hours Where to run commands We run commands in a terminal: a window where you type instructions and the computer answers. You do not run these commands in your browser. If you use Windows: 1. Press Windows key 2. Type Command Prompt 3. Click Command Prompt to open it You will see C:\Users\YourName If you use Mac: 1. Press Cmd + Space 2. Type Terminal 3. Press Enter You will see yourname@Mac ~ % If you use Linux: 1. Press Ctrl + Alt + T You will see yourname@laptop:~$ That line is called a prompt. It means the computer is waiting for you to type. Definitions for this class - Terminal: The app where you type commands. - Command: A typed instruction, such as ping google.com. - Internet: Networks that let computers communicate. - IP address: A numeric address used to find a device on a network. - DNS: Like a contacts list: it helps find the IP address for a name such as google.com. - Server: A computer or program that waits for and answers requests. - Ping: A basic test that sends a message and waits for a reply. - Nslookup: A command that asks DNS for information about a name. - Domain: A readable name, such as coraxreads.com. Step 1: Check internet with an IP In your terminal, type this and press Enter: What it does: Sends a small ICMP test message to the IP address 8.8.8.8. Because this command uses an IP address directly, it does not need to look up a domain name first. A reply tests one network path; it does not prove that every internet service works. Expected output on Windows: Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=25ms TTL=115 On Windows it stops by itself after 4 replies. Expected output on Mac or Linux: 64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp seq=1 ttl=115 time=25.123 ms On Mac or Linux it keeps going. Press Ctrl + C to stop it. What it means: A reply means that this destination responded to the network test. Your time and address may differ. If there is no reply, ICMP may be blocked; use the other checks before deciding the internet is down. If you see Request timed out or Network is unreachable, it does not automatically mean Wi-Fi is off. A network may block ping messages. Check your connection, then try the DNS and browser checks below. Step 2: Check names with DNS You are still in your terminal. Type: What it does: First asks DNS to turn google.com into an IP, then pings that IP. Expected output on Windows: Pinging google.com [142.250.80.46] with 32 bytes of data: Reply from 142.250.80.46: bytes=32 time=24ms TTL=115 Expected output on Mac or Linux: PING google.com (142.250.80.46): 56 data bytes 64 bytes from 142.250.80.46: icmp seq=0 ttl=115 time=24.123 ms Press Ctrl + C to stop it. What it means: DNS worked. It turned the name into 142.250.80.46. Your IP will be different. That is okay. Google has many IPs. If you see could not find host or could not resolve host, the name lookup failed. If the name resolves but ping times out, the network may block ping replies; try opening a website in the browser or ask your instructor. Step 3: See DNS working with nslookup You are still in your terminal. Type: What it does: Asks your DNS server directly for the IP. Expected output: Server: 192.168.1.1 Address: 192.168.1.1 53 Non-authoritative answer: Name: google.com Addresses: 142.250.80.46 What it means: Server is the DNS resolver that answered. Yours will be different. The answer shows IPs for google.com. Addresses can change and a domain can have several. Draw it Draw 4 boxes: Browser - DNS - Server - App Under each, write one sentence in your own words. Then write 3 sentences: What happens when you type google.com and press enter? Push In your portfolio, in modules/01-essentials, push your diagram and your 3 sentences.

title: Class 2: App Architecture, VS Code, AI, Troubleshooting
text: Class 2: App Architecture, VS Code, AI, Troubleshooting Time: 2 hours Where to run commands You will run commands in two places today: 1. In your normal terminal, like in Class 1 2. Inside VS Code, in its integrated terminal. That is a terminal inside VS Code. Definitions for this class - Frontend: What the user sees. Example: HTML page. - Backend: The part that checks requests and does the work. Example: Node.js code that handles an order. - Database: Where data is stored. Example: PostgreSQL. - Architecture: How the parts are arranged and how they talk. - VS Code: The editor where we write code. - Integrated terminal: A terminal inside VS Code. Shortcut: Ctrl + ` on Windows, Mac, Linux. - Prompt: A typed instruction to AI. A good prompt includes context. - Troubleshooting: Finding what broke, fixing it, and writing it down. Part 1: App Architecture and Stack CoraxReads architecture in plain words: Frontend sends a request. Backend does the work. Database stores the data. Backend sends the answer back to Frontend. Two-tier: Frontend + Database. Frontend talks straight to Database. Simple, but hard to grow. Three-tier: Frontend + Backend + Database. Frontend talks to Backend, Backend talks to Database. This separation can make an app easier to grow and secure. It is the target architecture for CoraxReads. Picture a bookstore: the webpage is the shop window, the backend is the clerk who checks an order, and the database is the stock ledger. The browser should talk to the backend; it should not connect straight to the database. Example stack for CoraxReads: - Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript - Backend: Node.js + Express - Database: PostgreSQL Part 2: VS Code Editor Steps: 1. Open VS Code 2. Click File, then Open Folder. Open your portfolio folder. 3. Pick a theme you like: File, Preferences, Theme, Color Theme 4. Open integrated terminal: Top menu, Terminal, then New Terminal 5. In that terminal, run for your system: If you use Windows: whoami, then dir If you use Mac or Linux: whoami, then pwd, then ls What it does: whoami: Shows your username pwd: On Mac or Linux, shows your current folder ls: On Mac or Linux, lists files in current folder dir: On Windows, lists files in current folder Expected output: You see your username and your files. That proves it is your environment. Part 3: How to use ChatGPT AI is an assistant, not an answer machine. Rules: 1. Never paste passwords, keys, or secrets into AI. 2. Ask with context: What you did, what you expected, what you saw. 3. Verify every AI answer by running it and reading the output. 4. If AI is wrong, say so and fix it. Good prompt example: I ran ping google.com and got could not resolve host, but ping 8.8.8.8 works. What is most likely broken and how do I check it? Explain to a beginner. Bad prompt example: My code is not working. Fix it. Part 4: Troubleshooting like a Pro with AI tools 5 steps, every time: 1. Reproduce: Can you make the error happen again? 2. Read: Read the full error message, not just the first line. 3. Isolate: What changed last? What step broke? 4. Ask: Search or ask AI with full context. 5. Fix and document: Fix it, then write what broke and how you fixed it. Write one troubleshooting note today: One thing that broke and how you fixed it.

title: Class 3: Asking Questions, Review, Role Play
text: Class 3: Asking Questions, Review, Role Play Time: 2 hours Definitions for this class Stakeholder: A person who cares about the project but may not know tech. Example: A shop owner. Jargon: Tech words that a non-tech person does not know. Example: Saying IP address without explaining it. Template: A fixed structure you fill in every time. Part 1: Guidelines for asking questions effectively Use this template every time: 1. What I was trying to do: 2. What I did: 3. What I expected: 4. What I saw instead, copy the exact error: 5. What I already tried: Bad question: My code is not working. Good question: I was trying to open my VS Code terminal and run dir. I clicked Terminal, then New Terminal. I expected to see my files. I saw the terminal did not open. I already tried closing and reopening VS Code. If you ask like this, you get help fast. title: Quiz Week 1: Knowledge Test
text: Quiz Week 1: Knowledge Test 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Score 90 percent, 11 out of 12, earns Week 1 Badge. One retake if below. Rules Do not look at answers before you try. Every question is from a lab we did this week. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE You run ping 8.8.8.8 and get replies. You run ping google.com and get could not resolve host. What is most likely broken? A. Internet cable B. DNS C. VS Code D. Your browser cache Answer: B. Explanation: Correct is B because ping to IP works, so internet works. Ping to name fails, so the name to IP step, which is DNS, is broken. A is wrong because internet works for the IP. C is wrong because VS Code is not used for ping. D is wrong because browser cache does not affect ping. Q2 - Choose ONE You run nslookup google.com and see Server 192.168.1.1, Name google.com, Addresses 142.250.80.46. What did nslookup do? A. It turned the name into an IP by asking DNS B. It installed Google C. It checked your VS Code theme D. It changed your IP address Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because nslookup asks DNS for the IP. B is wrong because it does not install anything. C is wrong because theme is not related. D is wrong because it does not change your IP. Q3 - Choose ONE CoraxReads domain is coraxreads.com and server IP is 102.130.45.78. Which DNS record connects them? A. A record B. CNAME record C. MX record D. TXT record Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because A record maps a domain to an IPv4 address. B is wrong because CNAME maps a name to another name, not to an IPv4. C is wrong because MX is for mail. D is wrong because TXT is for text notes, not for IP mapping. Q4 - Choose ONE In a three-tier app, where does the business logic live? A. Frontend B. Backend C. Database D. Browser cache Answer: B. Explanation: Correct is B because Backend does the work. A is wrong because Frontend only shows the UI. C is wrong because Database only stores data. D is wrong because cache only stores copies. Q5 - Choose ONE A user sees Not Secure in the browser when opening a site. What is most likely missing? A. HTTPS B. DNS C. VS Code D. A domain Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP. B is wrong because if DNS was missing, the site would not load at all. C is wrong because VS Code is not used by the visitor. D is wrong because the user already typed a domain to reach the site. Q6 - Choose ONE In VS Code terminal on Windows, which command lists files in the current folder? A. dir B. ls C. pwd D. whoami Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because dir lists files on Windows. B is wrong because ls is for Mac or Linux. C is wrong because pwd shows the folder path, not the files. D is wrong because whoami shows your username. Q7 - Choose ONE Which ChatGPT prompt is best for learning? A. My code is not working. Fix it. B. I ran ping google.com and got could not resolve host, but ping 8.8.8.8 works. What is most likely broken and how do I check it? Explain to a beginner. C. Tell me everything about networking. D. Give me the answer. Answer: B. Explanation: Correct is B because it has context, what you did, what you saw, what you tried, and asks for a beginner explanation. A is wrong because it has no context. C is wrong because it is too broad. D is wrong because it has no context and does not help you learn. Q8 - Choose ONE You change one line and get an error. What is the first step? A. Read the full error message B. Delete the whole project C. Ask AI with no context D. Reinstall VS Code Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because the error message tells you what broke. B is wrong because you lose your work. C is wrong because AI cannot help without context. D is wrong because reinstalling does not fix a one-line error. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about packet switching? A. Packets can take different routes to the destination B. Packets are reassembled at the destination C. All packets always take the same route D. If one packet is lost, the whole internet fails Answers: A, B. Explanation: A is true because packets can travel by different paths. B is true because they are put back in order at the end. C is false because routes can differ. D is false because TCP can resend a lost packet. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about TCP/IP? A. TCP divides application data into segments B. IP addresses each packet C. TCP provides ordered delivery to the application D. HTTP is the same thing as TCP Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: A is true because TCP divides a byte stream into segments; IP then carries data in packets. B is true because IP uses source and destination addresses. C is true because TCP reorders received data and retransmits missing data where needed. D is false because HTTP is an application protocol that uses lower-level transport/network protocols. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which are good questions? A. I was trying to run dir in VS Code terminal. I clicked Terminal, then New Terminal. I expected to see my files. I saw no terminal. I tried reopening VS Code. B. My code is not working. C. I was trying to ping google.com. I ran ping 8.8.8.8 and it worked. I expected ping google.com to work. I saw could not resolve host. I tried checking WiFi. D. Fix this. Answers: A, C. Explanation: A is good because it has all 5 parts of the template. C is good because it has context and what was tried. B is bad because it has no detail. D is bad because it has no context. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about three-tier architecture? A. Frontend shows the UI B. Backend does the work C. Database stores the data D. Frontend talks directly to Database in three-tier Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: A is true, Frontend is the UI. B is true, Backend is the logic. C is true, Database stores data. D is false, in three-tier Frontend talks to Backend, Backend talks to Database. Direct Frontend to Database is two-tier. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 1 Badge Below 11: One retake allowed, review Class 1 and Class 2 first

title: Week 2: Linux for DevOps - Local, No Cloud Yet
text: Week 2: Linux for DevOps - Local, No Cloud Yet Time: 3 classes, 2 hours each. Quiz at end of Week 2. Rule: No AWS, no EC2, and no cloud account this week. Codespaces is our temporary practice environment, not a production server. Codespaces is a lab, not a cloud VM - A Codespace is a managed development environment; it is not the same as an EC2 virtual machine. - Forwarding port 80 gives you a route to the app. It does not give the Codespace a public IP address or create a cloud security group. - Keep forwarded ports Private for this lab. Make a port public only with instructor approval and only when you understand who can access it. - curl http://localhost checks the web server from inside the Codespace. It is not the same as asking an external service for your public IP. How Week 2 works Class 1: Linux intro + Setup + System control + File navigation + File System Hierarchy Class 2: Text editors + Package manager + Sudo + Permissions + Users and Groups + Compression Class 3: Processes + Networking + System Info + Shell Scripting + Project Finalization Where to run commands In Codespaces, the provided terminal is Linux. This lab uses service to manage Nginx in its container: - Start Nginx: sudo service nginx start - Check Nginx: sudo service nginx status - Test Nginx config: sudo nginx -t Some Linux virtual machines use systemctl instead. Use the command taught for the environment you are in. If the command is unavailable, stop and ask for help rather than guessing. Definitions for Week 2 Linux: The operating system we use for servers. Ubuntu: A version of Linux, beginner friendly. Terminal: Where you type Linux commands. Package manager: Tool to install software. On Ubuntu it is apt. Sudo: Run a command as admin. Example: sudo apt update Permission: Who can read, write, or run a file. Process: A program running right now. Shell Script: A file with Linux commands that run one after another. Nginx: A web server that serves your website. Web Root: The folder Nginx serves. On Ubuntu it is /var/www/html What you will build this week 1. Your local Ubuntu lab, verified 2. Your CoraxReads site deployed locally with Nginx, at localhost 3. Your maintenance drill report: logs, resources, recovery 4. Your first shell script that checks your server Pass check for Week 2 - You can navigate, create, copy, move, delete files with Linux commands - You can explain permissions with rwx in plain words - You can serve a practice page with Nginx and open it through a privately forwarded Codespaces port - You can check logs, check disk, check memory, and recover Nginx after a break - Your assignment folder is on GitHub Lessons - Class 1: Linux, setup, and navigation - Class 2: Editors, packages, permissions, and users - Class 3: Processes, networking, and scripts - Assignment 2 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 2 - Role plays: explain Nginx and maintenance drill Official reference - Ubuntu server documentation - Nginx beginner's guide

title: Assignment 2: Deploy CoraxReads Locally with Nginx + Maintenance Drill
text: Assignment 2: Deploy CoraxReads Locally with Nginx + Maintenance Drill Time: 120 to 180 minutes Level: Beginner to Intermediate Submit in: Your portfolio repo, in folder modules/02-linux/assignment-2 Rule: No AWS and no EC2. Use Codespaces as a temporary practice environment, not as a production server. Overview You will serve a practice page locally with Nginx, then act as an on-call engineer and do a maintenance drill. Scenario CoraxReads wants a site. You will serve a practice page in a Codespace with Nginx, personalize it, check health, logs, and resources, then recover from two safe practice failures. Learning Outcomes 1. Use Linux commands to navigate, create, and manage files 2. Explain permissions, users, and processes 3. Deploy a static site with Nginx locally 4. Check logs, resources, and ports 5. Break and fix Nginx safely, with test before restart Rules 1. Write in your own words. 2. Screenshots should show the relevant Codespace and terminal output. Use a display name; do not expose personal information you do not want to share. 3. Do not paste passwords, tokens, or keys. 4. Keep Tasks 1 to 9 in order. Task 1 - Setup and Verify Linux Steps: Run cat /etc/os-release, whoami, pwd, hostname, uptime, free -h, df -h What to submit: Screenshot 1 - Output of uptime, free -h, df -h Task 2 - Install Nginx Steps: Run sudo apt update, then sudo apt install -y nginx. Check the version with nginx -v, start it with sudo service nginx start, check it with sudo service nginx status, and test the page with curl -I http://localhost. What to submit: Screenshot 2 - Output of curl -I http://localhost showing a successful response, and the Nginx version. Task 3 - Personalize CoraxReads Steps: Create index.html with CoraxReads and a display name (a first name or chosen name is fine). For example: What to submit: Screenshot 3 - Output of cat /var/www/html/index.html. Do not include personal details you do not want to share. Task 4 - Deploy with Correct Permissions Steps: Keep the practice page owned by the administrator. Set directory permissions with sudo chmod 755 /var/www/html and page permissions with sudo chmod 644 /var/www/html/index.html. Check with ls -l /var/www/html, test with sudo nginx -t, and only if the test succeeds, run sudo service nginx restart. Verify with curl http://localhost. What to submit: Screenshot 4 - Output of ls -l /var/www/html and sudo nginx -t showing the syntax test succeeded. Task 5 - Networking and Service Check Steps: Run ip a, ip route, ping -c 4 google.com, sudo ss -tulpn, and sudo service nginx status. What to submit: Screenshot 5 - Output of sudo ss -tulpn and notes: Which process is listening on port 80? Is anything listening on port 22? In Codespaces, do not expect an SSH server on port 22; the VS Code connection does not require one. Note any listener you do not recognize and ask before stopping it. Task 6 - Logs and Resources Steps: curl http://localhost, sudo tail -n 30 /var/log/nginx/access.log, sudo tail -n 30 /var/log/nginx/error.log, uptime, free -h, df -h, sudo du -sh /var/ sort -h What to submit: Screenshot 6 - Output of access.log and error.log, plus notes: Were there errors? If yes, explain 1 example. If no errors, what does that mean? Were your curl requests visible? Which resource looks most critical, CPU, memory, or disk, and why? What happens if disk becomes 100 percent full? Task 7 - Break and Fix Drill 1 - Nginx Config This drill uses a temporary test file so you do not break the real Nginx site. 1. Create the test configuration: 2. Save a backup with sudo cp /tmp/nginx-lab.conf /tmp/nginx-lab.conf.backup. 3. Test it with sudo nginx -t -c /tmp/nginx-lab.conf. It should pass. 4. Open the temporary file with sudo nano /tmp/nginx-lab.conf and remove the semicolon after listen 8081. 5. Test again. It should fail. Restore the known-good copy with sudo cp /tmp/nginx-lab.conf.backup /tmp/nginx-lab.conf, then test again. It should pass. Do not restart Nginx during this drill; you are only testing a temporary file. What to submit: Screenshot 7 - The failed test and the passing test after restoring the backup, plus notes: What caused the failure? Why is testing before applying a change safer? Task 8 - Break and Fix Drill 2 - Missing Web Root Use an empty Codespace lab. Before starting, check that /var/www/html exists and /var/www/html backup does not. If the backup path already exists, stop and ask for help. 1. Move the web root aside: sudo mv /var/www/html /var/www/html backup. 2. Create an empty web root: sudo mkdir /var/www/html. 3. Show the HTTP status: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http code}\n' http://localhost. An HTTP error status is expected; curl itself may still exit successfully. 4. Restore the original folder safely: sudo rmdir /var/www/html (this only removes an empty directory), then sudo mv /var/www/html backup /var/www/html. 5. Verify the page with curl -I http://localhost. Do not use rm -rf for this exercise. Restore the original folder immediately. What to submit: Screenshot 8 - The HTTP status before and after restoring the web root, plus notes: What caused the error? How did you restore the site safely? Task 9 - LinkedIn Post Steps: Write LinkedIn post with sections: Linux, Nginx Deploy, Logs, Resources, Break and Fix. Add 1 screenshot of localhost site and 1 of recovery. Add credit: P.S. This post is part of CoraxShift DevOps Academy - Week 2. Learn by building: https://github.com/coraxshift-academy What to submit: Screenshot 9 - Published LinkedIn post plus URL. Submission Checklist - Tasks 1 to 9 in order - Screenshots 1 to 9, readable, with personal details hidden or limited to a chosen display name - No passwords, tokens, keys, or personal information you do not want to publish - All writing in your own words - LinkedIn post with CoraxShift credit Final Submission Submit your portfolio folder link for modules/02-linux/assignment-2 plus your LinkedIn post URL.

title: Class 1: Linux Intro, Setup, System Control, File Navigation
text: Class 1: Linux Intro, Setup, System Control, File Navigation Time: 2 hours Where to run commands You are in Codespace terminal. You are already in Ubuntu. Do not open another terminal. Definitions for this class OS: Operating System, the main software that runs your computer. Linux: An OS used for most servers. Ubuntu: A version of Linux. Distribution: A version of Linux. Ubuntu is one distribution. Terminal: Where you type Linux commands. Prompt: The line waiting for you to type. Example: codespace@... Directory: Another word for folder. Home: Your main folder. In Codespace it is /home/codespace Step 1: Check your Linux Type: cat /etc/os-release whoami pwd hostname What it does: cat /etc/os-release: Shows your Linux version whoami: Shows your Linux username. In Codespace it is codespace pwd: Shows your current folder hostname: Shows your computer name Expected output: PRETTY NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS" codespace /workspaces/coraxshift-devops-academy Your version numbers may be slightly different. That is okay. Step 2: System control commands Type: uptime free -h df -h What it does: uptime: How long the server has been on, and load free -h: Memory, in human numbers. h means human df -h: Disk space, in human numbers Expected output: uptime shows 1 hour, load average numbers free -h shows total, used, free, available df -h shows Size, Used, Avail, Use percent What it means: Your server has memory and disk. If disk is 100 percent full, logs stop, apps fail. Step 3: File navigation commands You are still in terminal. Type one by one: ls ls -la pwd mkdir -p practice/week2 cd practice/week2 pwd cd .. ls What it does: ls: List files ls -la: List all files, with details, including hidden files mkdir -p: Make folder, p means make parent folders too cd: Change directory. cd .. means go up one level Expected output: You see your folders. After mkdir and cd, pwd shows .../practice/week2. After cd .., pwd shows .../practice Step 4: File System Hierarchy Type: ls / ls /var ls /var/www What it does: Shows the top folders of Linux. Plain words: - / : The root, the top of everything - /home : Where users live - /etc : Where config files live. Example: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default - /var : Where logs and websites live. Example: /var/log/nginx, /var/www/html - /tmp : Temporary files Step 5: Create and read a file Type: echo "Hello CoraxShift" practice/week2/hello.txt cat practice/week2/hello.txt cp practice/week2/hello.txt practice/week2/hello-copy.txt mv practice/week2/hello-copy.txt practice/week2/hello-moved.txt ls practice/week2/ rm practice/week2/hello-moved.txt ls practice/week2/ What it does: echo : Write text into a file cat: Read a file cp: Copy a file mv: Move or rename a file rm: Delete a file Expected output: After cat, you see Hello CoraxShift. After ls, you see the files. After rm, the moved file is gone. Push Push your notes: What is Linux, what is your Ubuntu version, and what did ls / show?

title: Class 2: Editors, Package Manager, Sudo, Permissions, Users, Compression
text: Class 2: Editors, Package Manager, Sudo, Permissions, Users, Compression Time: 2 hours Where to run commands You are in Codespace terminal. You are already in Ubuntu. Definitions for this class Editor: An app to write files. In Linux we use nano. Package manager: Tool to install software. On Ubuntu it is apt. Sudo: Run as admin. Example: sudo apt update Permission: Who can read (r), write (w), run (x) a file. Owner: The user who owns the file. Group: A set of users who share permissions. Compression: Making files smaller to store or send. Example: tar, gzip, zip. Step 1: Text editor nano Type: nano practice/week2/note.txt What it does: Opens nano editor. Type: This is my first Linux note Save: Press Ctrl + O, press Enter, press Ctrl + X to exit. Then type: cat practice/week2/note.txt Expected output: You see your note. Step 2: Package manager and sudo Type: sudo apt update -y sudo apt install -y nginx nginx -v What it does: apt update: Refresh list of software apt install: Install software. -y means yes, do not ask again nginx -v: Shows Nginx version Expected output: The Nginx version is shown. Your version may be different. That is okay. We install only what this week's lab needs; Node.js comes later in the course. Do not run apt upgrade -y in Codespace unless you need it, it takes long. Step 3: File and Directory Permissions Type: ls -l practice/week2/note.txt chmod 644 practice/week2/note.txt ls -l practice/week2/note.txt What it does: ls -l: Shows permissions like -rw-r--r-- chmod: Change permissions Plain words for -rwxr-xr-x: First letter: - means file, d means folder Next 3: Owner can read, write, run. rwx Next 3: Group can read and run, not write. r-x Last 3: Others can read and run, not write. r-x chmod 755 means: Owner rwx, Group r-x, Others r-x. Common for directories that people need to enter and list. chmod 644 means: Owner rw-, Group r--, Others r--. Common for files that need to be read but not run. chmod 777 means everyone can do everything. Do not use it in production. It is unsafe. For this static practice page, keep the files owned by the administrator and let Nginx read them: sudo chmod 755 /var/www/html sudo chmod 644 /var/www/html/index.html Nginx needs to read the page; it does not need permission to change it. Avoid making the web server the owner of files it only serves. Step 4: Managing users and groups Type: whoami id groups cat /etc/passwd grep codespace What it does: id: Shows your user id and groups groups: Shows groups you belong to cat /etc/passwd: Shows users on the system Expected output: You see codespace user, with groups. Do not create a new user in Codespace unless you need to, your Codespace user is enough for Week 2. In a real VM, you would use sudo adduser newname to create a user. Step 5: Compression and Archive Type: cd practice/week2 tar -czf notes.tar.gz note.txt hello.txt ls -lh tar -tzf notes.tar.gz mkdir -p extract && tar -xzf notes.tar.gz -C extract ls extract/ cd ../.. What it does: tar -czf: Create a compressed archive. c means create, z means gzip, f means file tar -tzf: List what is inside, without extracting tar -xzf: Extract. x means extract Expected output: You see notes.tar.gz, smaller than the files. Extract folder has your files. For zip: sudo apt install -y unzip zip zip notes.zip practice/week2/note.txt unzip -l notes.zip Push Push your notes: Explain 755 vs 644 in your own words, and what chown does.

title: Class 3: Processes, Networking, System Info, Shell Scripting, Project
text: Class 3: Processes, Networking, System Info, Shell Scripting, Project Time: 2 hours Where to run commands You are in Codespace terminal. You are already in Ubuntu. Definitions for this class Process: A program running right now. Port: A number door for network traffic. Example: 80 for HTTP, 22 for SSH. Log: A file that records what happened. Example: /var/log/nginx/access.log Shell Script: A file with Linux commands that run one after another. Nginx: Web server that serves your website. Web Root: Folder Nginx serves. /var/www/html Step 1: Monitoring and controlling processes Type: ps aux head -n 20 ps aux grep nginx grep -v grep top -b -n 1 head -n 20 What it does: ps aux: List processes grep nginx: Filter only nginx lines top: Show live processes, sorted by CPU. -b means batch, -n 1 means run once To stop a process, you use kill with the PID. Do not kill random processes in Codespace. We only practice with nginx. Type: sudo service nginx start ps aux grep nginx Expected output: You see nginx master and worker processes. Step 2: Networking commands in Linux Type: ip a ip route ping -c 4 google.com sudo ss -tulpn curl -I http://localhost What it does: ip a: Shows network interfaces and IPs ip route: Shows default gateway ping -c 4: Send 4 test messages. -c means count ss -tulpn: Shows listening ports and process names. t means TCP, u means UDP, l means listening, p means process, n means numbers curl -I: Shows headers only, to check if site works Expected output: ip a shows your interfaces ping shows 4 replies, 0 percent loss ss shows Nginx listening on port 80 curl shows HTTP/1.1 200 OK If curl shows 200 OK, Nginx is working. Step 3: System Information Commands Type: hostname lsb release -a uptime free -h df -h sudo du -sh /var/ sort -h What it does: hostname: Computer name lsb release -a: Ubuntu version uptime: How long server has been on free -h: Memory df -h: Disk du -sh: Size of folders inside /var, sorted Expected output: You see your hostname, Ubuntu 24.04, memory, disk, and /var folders sorted. Step 4: Shell Scripting Introduction Type: nano practice/week2/check.sh Paste this inside nano, save with Ctrl + O, Enter, Ctrl + X: !/bin/bash echo "Checking CoraxShift server..." uptime free -h df -h curl -I http://localhost Then type: chmod +x practice/week2/check.sh ./practice/week2/check.sh What it does: !/bin/bash: Tells Linux this is a bash script chmod +x: Make it runnable ./check.sh: Run it Expected output: You see Checking..., uptime, memory, disk, and HTTP 200 OK. Step 5: Project Finalization - Deploy CoraxReads locally Type: sudo apt install -y nginx sudo service nginx start echo '

title: Quiz Week 2: Linux for DevOps
text: Quiz Week 2: Linux for DevOps 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Score 90 percent, 11 out of 12, earns Week 2 Badge. One retake if below. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE You run ls -l and see -rwxr-xr-x for a file. What does it mean? A. Owner can read, write, run. Group and others can read and run. B. Everyone can do everything. C. No one can read it. D. It is a folder. Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because rwx is owner, r-x is group, r-x is others. B is wrong because 777 would be everyone can do everything. C is wrong because r means read is allowed. D is wrong because file starts with -, folder starts with d. Q2 - Choose ONE Which command shows your current folder? A. pwd B. ls C. cd D. whoami Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because pwd prints working directory. B is wrong because ls lists files. C is wrong because cd changes folder. D is wrong because whoami shows username. Q3 - Choose ONE Which command installs Nginx on Ubuntu? A. sudo apt install -y nginx B. npm install nginx C. pip install nginx D. git clone nginx Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because apt is Ubuntu package manager. B is wrong because npm is for Node packages. C is wrong because pip is for Python packages. D is wrong because git clone downloads code, does not install Nginx. Q4 - Choose ONE In Codespace, which command starts Nginx? A. sudo service nginx start B. sudo systemctl start nginx C. sudo nginx -t D. sudo apt update nginx Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because Codespace container uses service, not systemctl. B is wrong because systemctl does not work in Codespace container. C is wrong because nginx -t only tests config, does not start. D is wrong because apt update only refreshes list. Q5 - Choose ONE Which chmod gives owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x? A. chmod 755 B. chmod 644 C. chmod 777 D. chmod 600 Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because 7 is rwx, 5 is r-x, 5 is r-x. B is wrong because 644 is rw-, r--, r--. C is wrong because 777 is rwx for all, unsafe. D is wrong because 600 is rw- for owner only. Q6 - Choose ONE Which command shows running processes? A. ps aux B. ls -la C. pwd D. ip a Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because ps lists processes. B is wrong because ls lists files. C is wrong because pwd shows folder. D is wrong because ip a shows network. Q7 - Choose ONE Which command shows listening ports and process names? A. ss -tulpn B. ls -la C. free -h D. df -h Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because ss shows sockets. B is wrong because ls shows files. C is wrong because free shows memory. D is wrong because df shows disk. Q8 - Choose ONE Which is the correct first line of a bash script? A. !/bin/bash B. !bash C. bash D. !/bin/python Answer: A. Explanation: Correct is A because it tells Linux to use bash. B is wrong because path is missing. C is wrong because it is just a comment. D is wrong because it would use Python, not bash. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about Linux file system? A. / is the root, top of everything B. /etc holds config files C. /var holds logs and websites D. /home holds user folders Answers: A, B, C, D. Explanation: All are true. A is true, / is root. B is true, /etc has Nginx config. C is true, /var/log and /var/www. D is true, /home has users. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about Nginx config test? A. sudo nginx -t tests syntax B. If it says syntax is ok, config is valid C. If you remove the semicolon from listen in the temporary lab config, nginx -t fails D. You should restart Nginx without testing in production Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: A is true, -t tests. B is true, ok means the config passed this syntax test. C is true, a missing semicolon is a syntax error. D is false, test before applying a change. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about logs? A. /var/log/nginx/access.log shows requests B. /var/log/nginx/error.log shows errors C. journalctl -u nginx shows service logs in a VM D. Empty error log means server is permanently perfect Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: A is true, access log shows requests. B is true, error log shows errors. C is true, journalctl shows service logs. D is false, empty means no errors in that time period, not forever perfect. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply You are serving a static HTML page from /var/www/html. Which are good permission practices? A. Let the web server read the page without owning or changing it B. Use 755 for the directory and 644 for the HTML file C. Use chmod 777 so nobody gets blocked D. Verify the permissions with ls -l Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: A is true because a static web server needs to read the page, not edit it. B is true because the directory needs execute (enter) permission and the HTML file needs read permission. C is false because 777 allows everyone to change files. D is true because checking confirms what permissions are actually set. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 2 Badge Below 11: One retake allowed, review Class 1 and Class 2 first

title: Role Play 2: Setting up Nginx Web Server for Mini Finance
text: Role Play 2: Setting up Nginx Web Server for Mini Finance Time: 15 minutes in Class 3 Scenario A small finance shop wants a website. The owner asks: What is Nginx? Why do we need it? Can you set it up? Your job Explain Nginx in 1 minute, in plain words, no jargon. Use a waiter example: Nginx is like a waiter who takes orders and brings food from the kitchen to the customer. Example script in your own words When you open a website, your browser asks for a page. Nginx is the waiter. It takes your request, goes to the kitchen, which is the folder /var/www/html, gets the page, and brings it to you. If the waiter is not working, you get no page. We start the waiter with service nginx start, and we test it with nginx -t. Pass check - You spoke for about 1 minute - You used no jargon without explaining it - The owner can repeat it back - You mentioned web root in plain words What to push Write your 1 minute script in your portfolio, in your own words.

title: Role Play 3: Production Maintenance Drill - On-Call Engineer
text: Role Play 3: Production Maintenance Drill - On-Call Engineer Time: 15 minutes in Class 3 Scenario Your CoraxReads site is live in Codespace. Your manager calls: Site is slow. What do you check first? Your job Explain in 1 minute what you check, in order, in plain words. Example script in your own words First I check if Nginx is running with service nginx status. Then I check logs with tail -n 30 /var/log/nginx/error.log to see errors. Then I check resources with free -h and df -h to see if memory or disk is full. Then I check which process is listening with sudo ss -tulpn. If I find a break, I fix it, test with nginx -t, restart, and check with curl -I http://localhost. In Codespaces, I do not expect an SSH server on port 22. Pass check - You listed checks in order - You used plain words for logs, memory, disk, port - You mentioned test before restart - You mentioned verify after fix What to push Write your drill script in your portfolio.

title: Week 2 Troubleshooting
text: Week 2 Troubleshooting What you see Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- apt cannot download packages Network/DNS issue or package mirror unavailable Check connectivity and retry later; do not add an unknown repository. service nginx start fails Nginx is not installed or config has an error Run nginx -t, then inspect sudo service nginx status and error logs. curl localhost says connection refused Nothing is listening on port 80 Check service status and sudo ss -tulpn; start Nginx if it is your lab. curl gives 403 Directory index is missing or access is denied Check /var/www/html/index.html exists and is readable; do not use mode 777. Browser port does not open Port was not forwarded, or is not visible to your account Forward port 80 and keep it Private. Confirm curl http://localhost works inside the Codespace first. systemctl fails in Codespaces The container may not use systemd Use the Week 2 service commands in Codespaces; use the VM-specific command only on a full VM. Nginx syntax test fails Typo, missing semicolon, or invalid directive Read the file/line in the error, restore the last known-good config, run nginx -t again. ss shows a port you do not recognize Another lab or Codespaces service may be listening Record it and ask before stopping anything. Do not kill unknown processes. Page is missing after the drill The backup folder was not restored Stop editing, check /var/www/html backup, and follow the restore steps. Never delete the only backup. First-response sequence Capture the exact error and command. Do not paste private access tokens, keys, or personal account information into a public issue or screenshot.

title: Week 3: Bash for DevOps
text: Week 3: Bash for DevOps Project: CoraxReads Goal: Replace repeated, error-prone terminal work with small scripts that explain what they do and stop safely when something fails. What you will ship - scripts/healthcheck.sh checks the local practice site. - scripts/backup.sh creates a dated backup without overwriting the previous one. - A README section that explains how to run each script and what success looks like. Before you start - Finish the Week 2 Nginx lab, or use any local folder and HTTP endpoint. - Open the terminal in your portfolio project. - Run pwd to check where you are. pwd prints the current directory. Three classes 1. Shell building blocks: variables, quoting, input, and exit codes. 2. Reusable automation: functions, conditions, loops, and safe file handling. 3. Operations scripts: health checks, backups, logs, and troubleshooting. Scripts are not magic. They are saved instructions. Read a script before running it, especially when it uses sudo, changes files, or deletes data. Completion check - Scripts quote paths and fail on errors. - A health check exits non-zero when its check fails. - Backups have unique names and can be listed and restored. - No script stores passwords, API keys, or cloud credentials. Lessons - Class 1: Bash building blocks - Class 2: Safe automation - Class 3: Health checks and backups - Assignment 3 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 3 Official reference - GNU Bash manual

title: Assignment 3: Automate a Small CoraxReads Operation
text: Assignment 3: Automate a Small CoraxReads Operation Time: 2-3 hours Submit in: your portfolio repo, modules/03-bash/assignment-3/. Goal Deliver a health check and backup script that a teammate can run without guessing. The scripts must explain failures and must not silently overwrite data. Task 1 - Plan the scripts 1. Write down the directory you will back up and the local URL you will check. 2. Run pwd and ls -la to verify your location and current files. 3. Create scripts/ if needed with mkdir -p scripts. ls -la lists visible and hidden files with details. Do not run a script from a directory you did not intend to change. Task 2 - Build the health check 1. Create scripts/healthcheck.sh using the Class 3 example. 2. Add a useful error message to stderr. 3. Make it executable with chmod +x scripts/healthcheck.sh. 4. Run it against Nginx: ./scripts/healthcheck.sh http://localhost. 5. Stop Nginx with sudo service nginx stop; run the check and record the non-zero exit; restart it with sudo service nginx start; run the check again. This deliberate stop is limited to your practice server. Do not run it on a shared or production server. Task 3 - Build and test a backup 1. Create two sample files under practice-data/. 2. Create a timestamped archive under backups/ using tar -czf. 3. List the archive using tar -tzf. 4. Restore to a new directory and use diff -r practice-data restore-test/practice-data to compare them. diff -r compares directory contents recursively; no output means the files match. Task 4 - Explain and submit Submit both scripts, a README with run commands and expected results, and a short note explaining one failure you caused and how you verified recovery. Remove personal data and secrets before pushing. Pass checklist - Health check returns success for a healthy site and failure for a stopped site. - Backup names are unique. - Restore test matches the source. - Scripts quote paths and do not contain credentials or destructive wildcard deletion.

title: Class 1: Bash Building Blocks
text: Class 1: Bash Building Blocks Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your Codespace terminal, inside your portfolio repository. A script is a saved recipe An ingredient name in a recipe is like a variable; a step that depends on what you find is like an if. Bash runs these instructions in order. Create a practice folder and file: - mkdir -p scripts creates the directory and does not complain if it already exists. - printf writes predictable text to a file. replaces the file; appends. - cat prints a file so you can verify what was written. Create scripts/hello.sh: - The first line asks the environment to find Bash. - set -euo pipefail stops on command errors, unset variables, and failed commands inside pipelines. - ${1:-learner} uses the first argument, or learner if none was supplied. - Quotes around "$name" keep spaces together as one value. Run and compare: Expected output: Hello, A learner. Welcome to CoraxReads. Exit codes Every command returns a status: 0 usually means success, and non-zero means something went wrong. $? is the previous command's status. Check it immediately; the next command replaces it. Practice Change the script to accept a bookstore name as argument two. Test it with both arguments and with no arguments. Do not use eval to build commands from user input.

title: Class 2: Safe Automation
text: Class 2: Safe Automation Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your portfolio repository terminal. Conditions and functions - function name() { ... } groups reusable commands. - local limits a variable to the function. - [[ -f ... ]] checks for a regular file. - &2 sends the error message to stderr, separate from normal output. - return 1 marks the function as failed. Loops for repeats a block for each item; wc -l counts lines; < sends a file to a command as input. Safe file changes Before changing a file, inspect it with ls -l path and cat path. Use a new, exact output path for generated files. Do not use rm -rf in a beginner script. Prefer moving a known file to a dated backup, then verify the backup exists before proceeding. Never turn a variable into a command using eval. Never paste secrets into a script or commit .env files. Practice Write a script that accepts a source directory and a backup directory. Check that the source exists, refuse to overwrite a backup directory, and print the exact paths before copying. Use cp -a "$source" "$backup" to preserve file metadata. cp -a copies a directory tree and preserves attributes. Quoting each variable protects paths containing spaces.

title: Class 3: Health Checks and Backups
text: Class 3: Health Checks and Backups Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the Codespace that has the Week 2 Nginx lab. HTTP health check Create scripts/healthcheck.sh: - curl requests the URL. - --fail returns failure for HTTP 400 or 500 responses. - --silent --show-error suppresses progress but keeps error details. - --output /dev/null discards the page body. - exit 1 tells a later automation step that the check failed. Run it: chmod +x adds execute permission. Expected result: Healthy: http://localhost. Dated backup Create a backup of a small practice folder: - date creates a timestamp so backups have different names. - tar -czf creates a gzip-compressed archive at the path in $backup. - tar -tzf lists archive contents without extracting them. Do not delete the source folder after making the backup. A backup is useful only if you can restore it. Test restore into a new folder with tar -xzf "$backup" -C restore-test after creating restore-test. Review Explain what makes a health check fail, how a backup name avoids overwriting, and how you verified the archive.

title: Quiz Week 3: Bash for DevOps
text: Quiz Week 3: Bash for DevOps 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does exit status 0 usually mean? A. Success B. The script was deleted C. The computer restarted D. The output is empty Answer: A. Explanation: Zero conventionally means success; non-zero indicates an error or special condition. Q2 - Choose ONE Why quote "$backup"? A. To keep spaces in the path together B. To make the file executable C. To hide errors D. To compress the archive Answer: A. Explanation: Quoting prevents spaces and wildcard characters in a path from being split or expanded unexpectedly. Q3 - Choose ONE What does set -u help detect? A. Use of an unset variable B. A full disk C. A stopped service D. A Git conflict Answer: A. Explanation: -u makes Bash report references to unset variables instead of treating them as empty. Q4 - Choose ONE Which option makes curl fail for HTTP error statuses? A. --fail B. --output C. --silent D. --location Answer: A. Explanation: --fail gives curl a non-zero status for HTTP 400 and 500 responses. Q5 - Choose ONE What does tar -tzf archive.tar.gz do? A. Lists archive contents B. Deletes the archive C. Starts Nginx D. Changes file permissions Answer: A. Explanation: t lists, z handles gzip, and f names the archive file. Q6 - Choose ONE What should you do before restoring a backup? A. Restore to a separate test directory and compare B. Delete the original immediately C. Make the archive executable D. Rename the archive to .sh Answer: A. Explanation: A separate restore test proves the backup is usable without risking the original. Q7 - Choose ONE What does bash -n script.sh do? A. Checks syntax without executing B. Runs as root C. Prints environment secrets D. Compresses the script Answer: A. Explanation: The -n option parses the script but does not execute its commands. Q8 - Choose ONE Which is safest when accepting a path as an argument? A. Quote the variable and validate the path B. Pass it to eval C. Append to it D. Run rm -rf first Answer: A. Explanation: Quoting prevents splitting; validation ensures the script operates on the intended input. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which are useful script protections? A. set -euo pipefail B. Clear error messages to stderr C. Hard-coded cloud keys D. Quote variable expansions Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: Strict mode, clear errors, and quoting reduce common failures; credentials must not be embedded. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which commands help verify a backup? A. tar -tzf B. Restore into a separate directory C. Compare restored and source files D. Delete the source first Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Listing, restoring, and comparing check that the archive contains usable data. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which statements about $? are true? A. It is the previous command's status B. Check it before another command changes it C. It always contains the current directory D. Zero usually means success Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: $? is overwritten after each command, and zero usually signals success. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply Which are unsafe script practices? A. Using eval with untrusted input B. Quoting path variables C. Deleting a broad wildcard path without review D. Testing restore in a new directory Answers: A, C. Explanation: Dynamic command construction and broad deletion can execute or remove unintended targets. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 3 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 3 Troubleshooting
text: Week 3 Troubleshooting What you see Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- Permission denied Script is not executable or parent directory is not accessible Run ls -l scripts/healthcheck.sh; use chmod +x on the script, then run it with bash if needed. unbound variable set -u found a variable with no value Check spelling and provide a default such as ${1:-http://localhost}. URL appears as multiple arguments A path or URL was not quoted Quote variable expansions: "$url". curl returns success for an error page --fail was omitted Add --fail; test with an HTTP error response. Backup archive is empty Wrong working directory or source path Run pwd and ls -la on the source; create and list the archive again. tar says file changed as we read it Source was being edited during backup Stop writes during the lab and make a new timestamped archive. Backup would replace an earlier file Timestamp granularity or fixed name Include hours/minutes/seconds and check the destination before writing. Script stopped without a clear message A command failed under set -e Run with bash -x scripts/name.sh to print each command; do not paste secret values from debug output. Debugging commands - bash -n scripts/name.sh checks shell syntax without running the script. - bash -x scripts/name.sh traces commands as they run. - echo "$?" prints the previous command's exit status. - file scripts/name.sh shows the file type and may reveal Windows line endings. If you see ^M or a bad interpreter error, convert the file to Unix line endings in your editor and rerun bash -n.

title: Week 4: Git and GitHub
text: Week 4: Git and GitHub Project: CoraxReads Goal: Make small, reviewable changes and collaborate without losing work. What you will ship - A repository with a clear README and .gitignore. - A feature branch, a small commit, and a pull request. - A documented merge-conflict resolution. Three classes 1. Git basics: working tree, staging area, commits, and history. 2. Team workflow: branches, pull requests, code review, and conflicts. 3. Recovery and hygiene: restore, revert, ignore rules, and safe collaboration. Git is the notebook of changes; GitHub hosts the notebook and review conversation. Before you start Install Git and configure your name/email for commits. Never put passwords or access tokens in repository files or commit messages. Completion check - You can show the difference between unstaged and staged changes. - Your commit contains only the intended files. - You can explain how a pull request is reviewed and merged. - You know the difference between restore (discard local edits), revert (new undo commit), and reset (move a branch pointer). Lessons - Class 1: Git's three areas - Class 2: Branches and pull requests - Class 3: Conflict resolution and recovery - Assignment 4 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 4 Official reference - Pro Git book - GitHub: About pull requests

title: Assignment 4: Ship a Reviewed Change
text: Assignment 4: Ship a Reviewed Change Time: 2-3 hours Submit in: your portfolio repository, modules/04-git/assignment-4/. Task 1 - Check the repository Run git status, git branch --show-current, and git log --oneline -5. - status shows work not committed. - branch --show-current identifies your current work lane. - log shows recent snapshots. Write down the default branch and whether the working tree is clean. Do not continue if you have uncommitted changes you do not understand. Task 2 - Make a branch Run git switch -c docs/coraxreads-runbook. Add a short RUNBOOK.md with how to start the current practice app, how to check it, and how to ask for help. Task 3 - Review and commit Run git status, git diff, git add RUNBOOK.md, and git diff --cached. Confirm only your intended file is staged. Commit with a clear message. Task 4 - Open a pull request Run git push -u origin docs/coraxreads-runbook. Open a PR, describe the change and verification, and request a review. Do not merge until the reviewer approves. Task 5 - Practice conflict and recovery In a disposable file or toy repository, create a conflicting edit, resolve it, and record the resolution. Demonstrate git revert on a disposable commit. Do not use reset --hard on your portfolio. Submit Provide the PR link, screenshots of the staged diff and review, the conflict explanation, and the final runbook.

title: Class 1: Git's Three Areas
text: Class 1: Git's Three Areas Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your portfolio repository terminal. Picture the workflow Git does not automatically include every file in a commit. You choose what goes into the next snapshot. Inspect before changing - git status shows branch name and changed/untracked files. - git log --oneline -5 shows the five latest commits in compact form. Create and inspect a file: git diff shows tracked-file edits. A new untracked file will not appear in ordinary git diff; git status reports it. Stage one file and inspect the staged snapshot: git add selects content for the next commit; --cached shows exactly what is staged. Commit the change: A commit is a named snapshot. Use a message that says what changed and why. Practice Make a second edit after staging. Compare git diff and git diff --cached. Explain why the two outputs can differ.

title: Class 2: Branches and Pull Requests
text: Class 2: Branches and Pull Requests Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your portfolio repository. A branch is a safe work lane - git switch -c creates a branch and moves you onto it. - git branch --show-current confirms which branch will receive new commits. Edit one file, then review and commit: Replace path/to/changed-file.md with the exact path shown by git status. Publish the branch: -u remembers the remote branch so later git push commands know where to send commits. On GitHub, open a pull request into the default branch. Explain the goal, the change, and how you tested it. Review as a teammate Read the diff, ask questions about behavior, and check the tests. A review is about the change, not the person. Do not approve a change you have not read. Practice Open a pull request with one small documentation improvement. Ask a classmate to leave one question and one suggestion. Respond, update the branch, and observe that the PR updates automatically.

title: Class 3: Conflict Resolution and Recovery
text: Class 3: Conflict Resolution and Recovery Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your portfolio repository. Simulate a conflict safely Use a throwaway folder or ask a partner to edit the same line in separate branches. A conflict means Git cannot decide which of two edits is intended. Open each conflicted file. Git marks the competing versions with <<<<<<<, =======, and . Edit the file so it contains the intended final text and no markers remain, then run: git diff --check finds whitespace mistakes; review the final diff before staging. git add tells Git the conflict is resolved. Three ways to undo - choose carefully - git restore file discards unstaged edits to a file. This can destroy work. - git revert <commit makes a new commit that reverses a previous commit. It is usually safest for shared history. - git reset moves the current branch pointer and can rewrite local history. Do not use it to repair shared history without instructor guidance.
