Before recovery, run git status and save a copy of important work outside the repository. Practice Create a conflict in a throwaway file, resolve it, and explain which version you kept. Do not create a conflict in the course repository's real lesson files.

title: Quiz Week 4: Git and GitHub
text: Quiz Week 4: Git and GitHub 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does git status show? A. Working tree and staging state B. Internet speed C. Installed packages D. Server memory Answer: A. Explanation: Status shows changed, staged, and untracked files plus branch information. Q2 - Choose ONE What does git add do? A. Selects changes for the next commit B. Publishes a website C. Deletes history D. Opens a pull request Answer: A. Explanation: git add stages selected content; it does not commit or push it. Q3 - Choose ONE What does git diff --cached show? A. Staged changes B. Remote server logs C. Only deleted branches D. All file contents Answer: A. Explanation: The cached (staged) diff previews what the next commit will include. Q4 - Choose ONE Why make a feature branch? A. To isolate work for review B. To encrypt files C. To install GitHub D. To hide a secret in history Answer: A. Explanation: Branches let changes develop and be reviewed independently of the default branch. Q5 - Choose ONE Which undo operation is generally safest for shared history? A. git revert B. git reset --hard C. Delete .git D. Force-push Answer: A. Explanation: Revert records a new commit that reverses an earlier change. Q6 - Choose ONE What is a pull request primarily for? A. Review and discussion before merging changes B. Downloading a password C. Starting a Linux service D. Compressing a folder Answer: A. Explanation: A PR gives teammates a place to inspect and discuss a proposed change. Q7 - Choose ONE What should you review before committing? A. git diff --cached B. Browser cookies C. DNS cache only D. System uptime Answer: A. Explanation: It shows the exact staged content that the commit will capture. Q8 - Choose ONE You staged the wrong file but want to keep its edits. What should you do? A. git restore --staged FILE B. git restore FILE C. rm -rf .git D. git push --force Answer: A. Explanation: Restore staged removes it from the index while preserving working file content. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which commands inspect local Git state? A. git status B. git log --oneline C. git diff D. ping Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Status, log, and diff inspect repository state; ping tests network reachability. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply What should you do when resolving a text conflict? A. Read both versions B. Edit the intended final content C. Remove conflict markers D. Accept all changes without review Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: A conflict needs a deliberate final result; blindly accepting can lose required work. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which are good commit practices? A. Make a focused change B. Use a clear message C. Include credentials for convenience D. Review staged content Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: Focus and review improve collaboration; credentials do not belong in Git. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply A secret was pushed to a remote repository. Which actions are appropriate? A. Revoke or rotate it immediately B. Notify the repository owner C. Assume deleting the visible line removes all copies D. Follow incident cleanup guidance Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: A published secret must be treated as compromised; history and clones can retain it. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 4 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 4 Troubleshooting
text: Week 4 Troubleshooting Problem Check Safe fix --- --- --- nothing to commit Run git status and git diff Confirm you edited and saved the file; untracked files need git add. Wrong files staged Run git diff --cached Before commit, unstage with git restore --staged path; the file contents remain. Push rejected Run git status -sb and inspect the remote/branch Fetch and integrate the shared branch using the team workflow; do not force-push shared branches. src refspec ... does not match Run git branch --show-current Check spelling and ensure the branch has a commit. Merge conflict Run git status and open each conflicted file Edit to the intended result, remove markers, git diff --check, stage resolved files, then commit/continue as instructed. Accidentally committed a secret Stop pushing and tell the instructor/owner Revoke/rotate the credential immediately. Removing it from the latest commit does not erase it from history or copies. Useful commands - git diff --cached reviews the next commit. - git restore --staged FILE unstages a file without discarding its edits. - git revert COMMIT creates a new undo commit. - git remote -v shows where fetch and push go. Never run git push --force on a shared branch to make a rejection disappear.

title: Week 5: Plan, Build, Test, Release
text: Week 5: Plan, Build, Test, Release Project: CoraxReads Goal: Turn a feature idea into a small, testable, reversible change. What you will ship - One feature issue with a user story and acceptance criteria. - A small implementation plan and test checklist. - A release note and rollback plan. A bookstore example Feature: a visitor can see a list of books. The acceptance check is not "it works"; it is specific: "Given books exist, when the visitor opens the catalog, book titles and prices are shown." Three classes 1. Requirements: user, problem, scope, and acceptance criteria. 2. Testing: test layers, reproducibility, and a useful bug report. 3. Release operations: versioning, release checklist, monitoring, and rollback. Completion check - Work is small enough to review. - Acceptance criteria describe observable behavior. - Tests match the criteria. - Release notes say what changed; rollback steps are practical. Lessons - Class 1: Turn an idea into a testable issue - Class 2: Test the behavior - Class 3: Release and learn - Assignment 5 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 5 Official reference - NIST Secure Software Development Framework

title: Assignment 5: Plan a CoraxReads Feature
text: Assignment 5: Plan a CoraxReads Feature Time: 2-3 hours Submit in: your portfolio repo, modules/05-sdlc/assignment-5/. Task 1 - Write the issue Choose one feature: book catalog, search, or health endpoint. Write the user story, at least three measurable acceptance criteria, explicit out-of-scope behavior, risks, and a reviewer. Task 2 - Plan the work Break the feature into small tasks. For each task, name the file or component, expected change, and check that proves completion. Draw the request flow with arrows and label the browser, app, and data store. Task 3 - Create test cases For each acceptance criterion, record starting state, action, and expected result. Include a normal case, an empty/missing case, and a dependency failure case. State whether each is unit, integration, or end-to-end. Task 4 - Prepare release and rollback notes Write a release checklist, a short release note, and rollback steps. Explain why the previous version might not work after an irreversible database change. Task 5 - Review Ask a partner to try to find ambiguity in the criteria. Revise the issue based on feedback. Submit Issue link or Markdown issue, request-flow diagram, test plan, release note, rollback plan, and a short reflection on one risk you discovered.

title: Class 1: Turn an Idea into a Testable Issue
text: Class 1: Turn an Idea into a Testable Issue Time: 2 hours Tools: GitHub Issues or a Markdown file in your portfolio. Start with the person and problem Weak request: "Build a good bookstore." Clearer user story: As a visitor, I want to browse available books so that I can decide what to read. Add acceptance criteria: 1. Given the catalog has books, when I open /books, each available book shows title and price. 2. Given the catalog is empty, the page explains that no books are available. 3. Given the service cannot reach its data store, it reports a helpful error without exposing credentials. Acceptance criteria describe outcomes a person can verify. They are not a list of implementation details. Define a small scope Write down: - In scope: display books already in the catalog. - Out of scope: checkout, payments, user accounts. - Risks: empty catalog, database unavailable, invalid price. - Owner and reviewer: who builds and who checks the work. Draw a simple flow: Break the work into tasks that can each be reviewed, for example: add sample data, add catalog endpoint, render the list, test empty result. Practice Write an issue for "show books by genre." Include one user story, at least three acceptance criteria, one out-of-scope item, and one risk.

title: Class 2: Test the Behavior
text: Class 2: Test the Behavior Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your project terminal. Think in layers - Unit test: one small function, such as formatting a price. - Integration test: two parts working together, such as app and database. - End-to-end test: a user flow through the running system. Tests answer different questions. A green unit test does not prove a real deployment works. Turn acceptance criteria into checks For each criterion write: starting state, action, expected result. Example: For a running service, a basic request check is: - curl sends an HTTP request. - --fail returns failure for HTTP error status codes. - --silent --show-error hides progress but keeps errors. Use the port your app actually listens on. Do not copy the example port without checking the app configuration. Bug reports Record: environment, exact steps, expected result, actual result, logs, and the smallest safe reproduction. Remove tokens, customer data, and private URLs before sharing. Practice Write one test case for a normal response, one for empty data, and one for the data store being unavailable. Mark which layer each test exercises.

title: Class 3: Release and Learn
text: Class 3: Release and Learn Time: 2 hours Tools: Git, GitHub, and your release checklist. Release checklist 1. Link the change to its issue. 2. Review the diff and test results. 3. Confirm required configuration is documented and secrets are not in Git. 4. Record the version and user-visible changes. 5. Deploy to a test environment, then check health. 6. Know how to restore the previous version. 7. Watch logs and metrics after release. Versioning and notes A release note tells users what changed and anything they need to do. A version such as v1.2.0 communicates a named release. In this course, use Git tags for milestones: - git tag -a creates an annotated release marker. - git show inspects the tag and its commit. Do not tag a release until the reviewed change is committed and tested. Rollback is a plan, not a button Write down the previous known-good version, who can approve rollback, what command or workflow restores it, and how to verify service health afterward. A database change may not be reversible just by switching application versions. Practice Make a release checklist for the catalog feature. Add one monitoring signal and one rollback risk.

title: Quiz Week 5: SDLC
text: Quiz Week 5: SDLC 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What makes acceptance criteria useful? A. They describe observable results B. They use the most technical words C. They guarantee no bugs D. They replace user needs Answer: A. Explanation: Observable criteria can be tested and reviewed. Q2 - Choose ONE Which test checks one small function? A. Unit test B. End-to-end test C. Capacity test D. Manual deployment Answer: A. Explanation: Unit tests focus on a small isolated piece of behavior. Q3 - Choose ONE What does an integration test check? A. Parts working together B. Only a function name C. GitHub account billing D. Laptop battery health Answer: A. Explanation: Integration tests check boundaries such as app-to-database behavior. Q4 - Choose ONE Why have rollback steps? A. To restore a known-good service if a release fails B. To erase code review C. To skip testing D. To delete logs Answer: A. Explanation: Rollback provides a practiced recovery path when a release causes problems. Q5 - Choose ONE What should a useful bug report include? A. Reproduction steps and expected/actual results B. A guess only C. A password D. No environment details Answer: A. Explanation: Reproducible evidence helps another person isolate the fault. Q6 - Choose ONE What does git tag -a create? A. An annotated named point in history B. A cloud server C. A database backup D. A firewall rule Answer: A. Explanation: A tag names a commit, often used to identify a release. Q7 - Choose ONE What is a release note for? A. Summarizing user-visible changes B. Storing API keys C. Replacing tests D. Hiding known risks Answer: A. Explanation: Release notes communicate changes and relevant user actions. Q8 - Choose ONE Which is a better criterion than "search works well"? A. Given matching books, search shows their titles B. Search is modern C. Search uses technology D. Search is nice Answer: A. Explanation: It describes a verifiable starting state and result. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply What belongs in a small feature plan? A. Scope B. Risks C. Acceptance checks D. A secret token Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Scope, risk, and checks guide work; secrets do not belong in planning artifacts. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are useful test-case details? A. Starting state B. Action C. Expected result D. An unrelated opinion Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: These three details make a test repeatable. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply What should happen before a release? A. Review the diff B. Check test results C. Know the rollback path D. Ignore configuration changes Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Review, tests, and recovery preparation reduce release risk. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply Why may rolling back code not be enough? A. Data migrations may not be reversible B. External side effects may have occurred C. The previous app may expect an older schema D. Git tags delete data automatically Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Data and external changes can outlive a code rollback; tags do not reverse them. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 5 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 5 Troubleshooting
text: Week 5 Troubleshooting Problem Why it happens What to do --- --- --- Acceptance criterion says "works well" It is subjective and cannot be tested Name the input, action, and visible expected result. Test passes but user flow fails The test checks a different layer or misses wiring/configuration Trace the request end to end; add an integration or user-flow test. Test depends on data from a previous run Test state is not isolated Create known test data before each run and clean up only that test data. Bug cannot be reproduced Steps or environment details are missing Capture exact inputs, versions, expected/actual result, and sanitized logs. Rollback restores app but not data A schema/data change was not backward-compatible Plan database migrations and compatibility before deployment; ask for review. When a test fails, preserve the first useful error. Do not make several speculative changes before recording what happened.

title: Week 6: Terraform Fundamentals
text: Week 6: Terraform Fundamentals Project: CoraxReads Goal: Describe local infrastructure in code, review a plan, and clean it up safely. What you will ship - Terraform configuration for a local Nginx container. - A saved plan and notes explaining what Terraform will create. - Evidence that the container responds and was destroyed afterward. Three classes 1. Infrastructure as code: providers, resources, and configuration. 2. State and review: init, validate, plan, apply, outputs, and drift. 3. Safe lifecycle: variables, destroy, state safety, and cost/security boundaries. Terraform state maps the code to real resources. Treat it as sensitive operational data; do not commit state files. Prerequisites - Docker Engine available in your local lab environment. - Terraform CLI installed. - Do not configure cloud providers this week. Keep the exercise local. Lessons - Class 1: Terraform and providers - Class 2: Plan before apply - Class 3: State and cleanup - Assignment 6 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 6 Official reference - Terraform documentation - Terraform Docker provider

title: Assignment 6: Provision a Local CoraxReads Web Container
text: Assignment 6: Provision a Local CoraxReads Web Container Time: 2-3 hours Submit in: your portfolio repo, modules/06-terraform/assignment-6/. Task 1 - Prepare safely 1. Confirm Docker works with docker version. 2. Confirm Terraform is installed with terraform version. 3. Create a clean folder and put the Class 1 configuration in main.tf. 4. Add .terraform/, .tfstate , .tfplan, and crash.log to .gitignore. docker version shows client and server information; if no server section appears, Docker Engine is not reachable. Task 2 - Validate and plan Run terraform fmt, terraform init, terraform validate, and terraform plan -out=lab.tfplan. Explain the purpose of each command in your notes. Save a sanitized plan excerpt; do not upload state. Task 3 - Apply and verify Read the plan. Confirm only one Nginx image and one named container are involved. Run terraform apply lab.tfplan, then terraform output and curl --fail http://localhost:8080. Task 4 - Change and review Change host port 8080 to 8081. Format and plan again. Predict whether the container will be replaced or updated based on the plan. Apply only after review, then verify port 8081. Task 5 - Destroy and verify Run terraform plan -destroy; confirm it refers only to the lab resource. Run terraform destroy, then docker ps -a to verify cleanup. Submit Terraform files, .gitignore, a plan summary, command explanations, HTTP check evidence, cleanup evidence, and one troubleshooting note. Exclude state, plans, credentials, and .terraform/.

title: Class 1: Terraform and Providers
text: Class 1: Terraform and Providers Time: 2 hours Run commands in: a new terraform-lab/ folder with Docker available. What Terraform does Terraform reads desired infrastructure from .tf files, asks a provider to compare that intent with the current environment, then proposes changes. Create the folder and configuration: In main.tf, put: - required providers declares which plugin Terraform needs. - provider "docker" configures the Docker connection using its defaults. - resource describes a managed image and container. - ports maps host port 8080 to container port 80. - output prints a helpful URL after apply. Review every resource before applying. This example only runs a local container.

title: Class 2: Plan Before Apply
text: Class 2: Plan Before Apply Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the terraform-lab/ directory. Run: - fmt formats Terraform files consistently. - init downloads the declared provider and creates local working metadata. - validate checks configuration structure and provider schemas. - plan previews changes; -out saves the exact plan for review/application. Read the plan. Check the names, ports, and actions. + means create, ~ means update, - means destroy. If Terraform proposes unexpected resources, stop and investigate. Apply the reviewed plan: - apply lab.tfplan applies the reviewed plan file. - output prints declared outputs. - curl verifies the web server answers. Do not use -auto-approve in a learning or production workflow until a reviewed automation design explicitly permits it.

title: Class 3: State, Drift, and Cleanup
text: Class 3: State, Drift, and Cleanup Time: 2 hours Run commands in: terraform-lab/. State is a map Terraform state records the resource identities it manages and links them to configuration. It is not a cache to casually delete. Never commit terraform.tfstate, saved plans, or files under .terraform/. Inspect: - state list names resources tracked in state. - show describes the current tracked resources. If someone changes infrastructure outside Terraform, the actual environment can drift from the code. A new terraform plan helps identify differences. Do not run terraform refresh or edit state by hand to hide drift. Destroy only the lab First verify the directory and workspace: pwd confirms location; workspace show identifies the active workspace; plan -destroy previews deletions. Read the plan and confirm it names only coraxreads-terraform-lab. Then clean up: Review the prompt before confirming. Verify the container is gone with docker ps -a. Practice Change the external port to 8081, format, validate, and plan. Explain the planned change before applying it.

title: Quiz Week 6: Terraform
text: Quiz Week 6: Terraform 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does a Terraform provider do? A. Connects Terraform to an API or platform B. Writes application tests C. Replaces Git D. Encrypts every source file Answer: A. Explanation: Providers implement resources and data sources for a platform. Q2 - Choose ONE What does terraform init do? A. Prepares the working directory and downloads providers B. Deletes all resources C. Starts a server D. Creates a Git commit Answer: A. Explanation: Init installs declared providers and sets up local working metadata. Q3 - Choose ONE Why run terraform plan? A. Preview proposed changes B. Skip state C. Expose a port D. Format HTML Answer: A. Explanation: Plan compares configuration/state and previews actions before applying. Q4 - Choose ONE What does terraform apply lab.tfplan apply? A. The saved plan file B. Every file in the folder C. A GitHub pull request D. A database backup Answer: A. Explanation: The command applies the reviewed plan named in the argument. Q5 - Choose ONE What does Terraform state do? A. Maps configuration to managed resource identities B. Stores all website images C. Replaces firewall rules D. Stores learner grades Answer: A. Explanation: State tracks the resources Terraform manages. Q6 - Choose ONE What should you do if plan proposes an unexpected deletion? A. Stop and investigate before applying B. Apply immediately C. Delete the state file D. Hide the plan Answer: A. Explanation: An unexpected deletion may indicate wrong workspace, state, or config. Q7 - Choose ONE What does terraform fmt do? A. Formats Terraform files B. Deploys a container C. Creates credentials D. Runs Nginx Answer: A. Explanation: Fmt normalizes configuration formatting. Q8 - Choose ONE What is safest before destroying a lab? A. Review the destroy plan and resource names B. Delete all state C. Run a wildcard Docker cleanup D. Ignore the active workspace Answer: A. Explanation: A reviewed plan limits accidental deletion to intended resources. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which artifacts should normally stay out of Git? A. Terraform state B. Saved plans C. .terraform/ directory D. A sanitized README Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: State/plans and provider cache can contain sensitive or generated data; docs can be committed after review. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which commands help review a Terraform lab? A. terraform validate B. terraform plan C. terraform state list D. rm -rf ~ Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Validate, plan, and state listing are focused review tools; broad deletion is unsafe. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply What should be checked when Docker provider cannot connect? A. Docker daemon availability B. docker version server section C. Whether the socket is exposed insecurely D. Cloud root password in source Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Provider access depends on Docker daemon connectivity; never put root credentials in code. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply What are good infrastructure-as-code habits? A. Review a plan before apply B. Keep state protected C. Investigate drift D. Apply every plan without reading Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Plans, protected state, and drift review improve safety; blind applies do not. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 6 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 6 Troubleshooting
text: Week 6 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- terraform: command not found Terraform CLI is missing or not on PATH Follow the official install instructions for your OS, reopen the terminal, then check terraform version. Docker provider cannot connect Docker daemon is stopped or socket is unavailable Run docker version; start Docker Engine or use a supported local VM. Do not expose the Docker socket over an unauthenticated network. terraform init fails Network/provider registry access or configuration typo Read the first provider error, check the source and version constraint, retry after network recovery. Plan wants to destroy unexpected resources Wrong directory/workspace/state or changed configuration Stop. Check pwd, terraform workspace show, state list, and plan. Do not apply. Port 8080 already allocated Another local service uses the port Find the listener with docker ps or ss -tulpn; choose a free host port and re-plan. terraform destroy cannot find a resource State and actual resources differ Inspect terraform state list and docker ps -a; do not delete state to make the error disappear. Never commit Terraform state or a saved plan. A plan can contain values that should not be public even when they are marked sensitive.

title: Week 7: Ansible Configuration Automation
text: Week 7: Ansible Configuration Automation Project: CoraxReads Goal: Describe a repeatable web-server setup as an Ansible playbook and safely apply it to a lab machine. What you will ship - An inventory for a practice Ubuntu target. - A playbook that installs Nginx and deploys a static CoraxReads page. - Evidence that a second run makes no unnecessary changes. Three classes 1. Inventory and playbooks: hosts, tasks, modules, and variables. 2. Repeatability: templates, handlers, idempotency, and privilege escalation. 3. Safe execution: syntax check, check mode, diff, and troubleshooting. Ansible is an instruction runner, not a backup system. Use a disposable lab target, keep changes reviewed, and never run an unreviewed playbook against production. Lessons - Class 1: Inventory and first playbook - Class 2: Idempotency and handlers - Class 3: Preview and apply safely - Assignment 7 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 7 Official reference - Ansible getting started - Ansible playbook guide

title: Assignment 7: Configure a Practice Web Server
text: Assignment 7: Configure a Practice Web Server Time: 2-3 hours Target: An Ubuntu VM or a disposable Ubuntu Codespace where you have admin permission. Task 1 - Prepare the target Run whoami, cat /etc/os-release, ansible --version, and sudo service nginx status. Confirm the OS, Ansible version, and target. If you are not sure which machine a command will affect, stop. Task 2 - Write the inventory and playbook Use the Class 1 inventory. Create a playbook with tasks to: 1. Install Nginx using the package module. 2. Create /var/www/html/index.html owned by root, mode 0644. 3. Ensure Nginx is started. Explain each module and the desired state in a comment or README. Avoid shell/command modules when an Ansible module already exists. Task 3 - Preview and apply Run inventory listing, syntax check, then --check --diff. Read the output. Apply only to the lab target. Task 4 - Verify and rerun Run curl -I http://localhost, inspect ls -l /var/www/html/index.html, and run the playbook again. Explain why the second run should make no changes. Task 5 - Break and recover Change the page text and run the playbook again. Confirm the page updates. Restore the original text and rerun. Do not remove system directories or test against production. Submit Inventory, playbook, README with each command explained, sanitized first/second run output, HTTP check, and one troubleshooting note. Exclude SSH keys and credentials.

title: Class 1: Inventory and First Playbook
text: Class 1: Inventory and First Playbook Time: 2 hours Run commands in: an Ubuntu lab machine where you have permission to use sudo. Inventory: where Ansible works Create inventory.ini: An inventory names hosts and groups. ansible connection=local runs modules on the same machine; it does not connect through SSH. Create site.yml: - hosts selects inventory members. - become: true requests elevated privileges for system changes. - apt declares the desired package state rather than a shell command. - copy writes the exact page and sets owner/mode. - service asks the platform's service manager to keep Nginx running. The ansible.builtin prefix identifies modules included with Ansible. Inspect before execution site.yml is YAML: indentation matters. Use spaces, not tabs. Review the playbook before running it because tasks can change the target.

title: Class 2: Idempotency and Handlers
text: Class 2: Idempotency and Handlers Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your Ansible lab folder. Idempotency means "make it so" A playbook should describe the desired result. If the machine already matches, a second run should make no changes. For example, apt with state: present installs Nginx if missing and leaves it alone if present. Use a template for changing content Create templates/index.html.j2: Add a variable such as environment name: lab under vars: in the play. Replace the copy task with: The template module fills placeholders with variables and writes the result. File mode 0644 allows the web server to read the page without giving it write access. Handler Handlers run only when notified by a changed task. Add notify: Validate and reload Nginx to a changed Nginx configuration task, then define: Do not reload a service merely because the playbook ran; tie the handler to a relevant change. Test the service behavior in your lab first.

title: Class 3: Preview and Apply Safely
text: Class 3: Preview and Apply Safely Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your Ansible lab folder. Check syntax and target selection - ansible-inventory --list displays the resolved hosts and groups. - --syntax-check parses the playbook without applying tasks. Preview where supported: - --check asks supported modules to predict changes. - --diff shows file changes that modules can preview. Check mode is not a perfect simulation. Some modules cannot predict results, so read output and review the playbook. Apply to the lab: On a remote host that requires a become password, add --ask-become-pass. Do not put that password in inventory or source code. Run the playbook a second time. A stable host should report zero changed tasks for work that is already correct.

title: Quiz Week 7: Ansible
text: Quiz Week 7: Ansible 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does an Ansible inventory describe? A. Hosts and groups to manage B. Git commit messages C. Database rows D. Browser history Answer: A. Explanation: Inventory identifies the target machines and groupings. Q2 - Choose ONE What does become: true request? A. Privilege escalation for tasks B. A new Git branch C. Public port forwarding D. A container image Answer: A. Explanation: Become asks Ansible to run tasks with elevated privileges where configured. Q3 - Choose ONE What is idempotency? A. Re-running desired-state automation does not keep changing a correct target B. A task runs forever C. A password is encrypted D. A server has no logs Answer: A. Explanation: Idempotent tasks converge the target and are stable on repeat runs. Q4 - Choose ONE What does --syntax-check do? A. Parses the playbook without applying tasks B. Starts all services C. Installs every package D. Commits YAML Answer: A. Explanation: Syntax check validates playbook structure without applying it. Q5 - Choose ONE Why use a handler? A. Run a service action only after a related task changes B. Store a password C. Open a browser D. Delete inventory Answer: A. Explanation: A handler is notified by changed tasks and runs at the appropriate time. Q6 - Choose ONE What does --check --diff provide? A. A preview of supported changes B. A guaranteed perfect simulation C. A cloud bill D. A secret scan only Answer: A. Explanation: Check mode previews supported tasks, but it is not complete simulation. Q7 - Choose ONE What does ansible.builtin.copy do? A. Copies content or a file to a target B. Creates a GitHub PR C. Restarts the laptop D. Encrypts Terraform state Answer: A. Explanation: The copy module manages file content on a target. Q8 - Choose ONE Where should a become password go? A. Prompt/approved secret mechanism, not committed YAML B. Public inventory C. Git commit message D. HTML source Answer: A. Explanation: Credentials must not be stored in tracked plain text. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply What helps make playbooks safer? A. Review the inventory target B. Run syntax check C. Use check mode where supported D. Apply to production first Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Target confirmation and previews reduce risk; production is not a practice target. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are true about modules? A. apt manages packages B. service manages services C. template renders variables into files D. Shell is always better than modules Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Built-in modules model common desired state; shell is not always idempotent. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply What should a learner do after the first apply? A. Verify the service response B. Inspect managed file permissions C. Run again and inspect changed count D. Assume success without checking Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Verification and a second run test both outcome and idempotency. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply Which values should not be committed? A. SSH private keys B. Plain-text passwords C. Public non-sensitive task names D. Cloud credentials Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: Private credentials must be protected; task names are not secrets. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 7 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 7 Troubleshooting
text: Week 7 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- ansible-playbook: command not found Ansible is not installed or PATH is stale Check ansible --version; install it in the chosen lab environment. could not match supplied host pattern Inventory path/group name is wrong Run ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --list; compare the group to hosts:. YAML syntax error Indentation, colon, or quote error Read the reported line and check surrounding indentation; run --syntax-check. Permission denied become missing or target user lacks sudo Confirm target and privilege policy; use --ask-become-pass if required. Never add passwords to YAML. Service task fails in a container Container has no compatible init/service manager Use a proper Ubuntu VM for service-management practice; do not install systemd blindly into the container. Every rerun reports changes Task is not idempotent or output changes each run Prefer declarative modules; remove timestamps/random content from managed files. Check mode says no change but real run changes Module does not fully support check mode Treat check mode as a hint; inspect module docs and review/apply only in the lab. Use -vv for extra task-level detail. Avoid -vvvv when output could expose connection details or sensitive values.

title: Week 8: Docker and Compose
text: Week 8: Docker and Compose Project: CoraxReads Goal: Build a small application image and run the app with PostgreSQL using Docker Compose. What you will ship - A Dockerfile for the CoraxReads app. - A Compose file for app + database. - A health check and evidence that database data survives a container restart. Three classes 1. Images and containers: build context, layers, ports, and logs. 2. Compose and networking: app, database, service names, volumes, health. 3. Safe images: non-root users, secrets, tags, and cleanup. Before you start - Install Docker Engine and the Compose plugin. - Use the course CoraxReads starter app; it includes /health, /api/books, tests, Dockerfile, and Compose. - Store local credentials in an ignored .env file; commit only a placeholder .env.example. Lessons - Class 1: Build an image - Class 2: Compose app and database - Class 3: Verify, secure, and clean up - Assignment 8 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 8 Official reference - Docker Get Started - Docker Compose documentation

title: Assignment 8: Containerize CoraxReads
text: Assignment 8: Containerize CoraxReads Time: 3-4 hours Submit in: your portfolio repository. Task 1 - Prepare the app Use the course starter in labs/coraxreads/ as your reference. Copy it into your portfolio repository or fork the course repository for the lab. Read labs/coraxreads/README.md. Run npm ci and npm test; confirm the health endpoint and catalog behavior in the source. Keep .env local and untracked. Task 2 - Write the Dockerfile Review the starter Dockerfile, adapt it only if your app differs, and explain each instruction. Confirm the app uses the non-root node user. Task 3 - Write Compose Review and run the starter compose.yaml. Identify the app and db services, private database network, named data volume, and health check. Set local values in .env using .env.example; do not commit .env. Task 4 - Build and test Run: Explain what each command verifies. Change port 3000 if your app uses another port. Task 5 - Prove persistence and clean up Create sample data. Run docker compose down, start again, and verify data remains. Then clean up containers. Keep the volume until the instructor confirms the evidence is complete; delete it only if the data is disposable. Submit Dockerfile, .dockerignore, compose.yaml, .env.example with placeholders, run instructions, test evidence, persistence evidence, and one troubleshooting note. Never submit .env.

title: Class 1: Build an Image
text: Class 1: Build an Image Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the folder containing your app's package.json. Image versus container An image is a packaged recipe; a container is a running copy. A Dockerfile describes how to build the image. Example Node Dockerfile: - FROM selects a base image. - WORKDIR sets the working folder inside the image. - Copying manifests before source allows dependency layers to be reused. - npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile records. - USER node avoids running the app as root. - EXPOSE documents the app's listening port; it does not publish that port. - CMD is the default process when a container starts. Create .dockerignore and exclude node modules, .git, .env, logs, and local build output. Build and inspect: docker build creates an image from the current build context; -t gives it a local name. Review the build context so secrets are not copied into an image.

title: Class 2: Compose App and Database
text: Class 2: Compose App and Database Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the folder with compose.yaml. Compose example - Compose creates a private network; the app reaches the database by service name db. - ports publishes only the app port to the host. The database has no host port mapping. - depends on waits for the database health check before starting the app. - A named volume keeps database files when the container is recreated. - $$ defers variable expansion to the container shell. Put local values in .env, add .env to .gitignore, and never commit real passwords. Use a unique random local password. Start and inspect: config renders/validates Compose; up builds and starts services in the background; ps shows state; logs shows recent app output.

title: Class 3: Verify, Secure, and Clean Up
text: Class 3: Verify, Secure, and Clean Up Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the Compose project directory. Verify the app and data - curl --fail checks HTTP success. - exec runs a command inside an already-running service. - pg isready asks PostgreSQL whether it accepts connections. - restart restarts only the named app service. Add a sample book through the app or SQL, restart the database, and verify data still exists. Do not remove volumes during the persistence test. Security checklist - Run the app as a non-root user. - Keep the database off host-published ports unless a lesson specifically needs access. - Do not bake .env into images. - Use a maintained base image and update it deliberately. - Do not use privileged: true to make permission problems disappear. Clean up down stops and removes Compose containers and network but keeps named volumes. Only after confirming the data is disposable may you remove the named volume with an explicit project-specific command. Volume deletion is irreversible.

title: Quiz Week 8: Docker and Compose
text: Quiz Week 8: Docker and Compose 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What is a Docker image? A. A packaged template used to create containers B. A running process only C. A Git branch D. A database backup Answer: A. Explanation: An image contains filesystem layers and metadata used to start containers. Q2 - Choose ONE What does EXPOSE 3000 do? A. Documents the container port; it does not publish it B. Opens the host firewall automatically C. Starts PostgreSQL D. Makes the app root Answer: A. Explanation: Host publication requires a runtime or Compose port mapping. Q3 - Choose ONE Why use npm ci in a build? A. Install versions from the lockfile reproducibly B. Update every dependency freely C. Start the server D. Expose port 3000 Answer: A. Explanation: npm ci uses the lockfile and is designed for clean automated installs. Q4 - Choose ONE How should a Compose app reach the database? A. By the database service name on the Compose network B. By guessing its public IP C. Through the user's browser D. By embedding a password in source Answer: A. Explanation: Compose service discovery resolves the service name on its private network. Q5 - Choose ONE What does a named volume provide? A. Persistent storage beyond container recreation B. Public internet access C. A Git tag D. An image build cache only Answer: A. Explanation: A volume stores data independently of a container's writable layer. Q6 - Choose ONE What does docker compose down normally preserve? A. Named volumes, unless --volumes is used B. Every container C. All host processes D. Image tags in Git Answer: A. Explanation: Down removes services/network but preserves named volumes by default. Q7 - Choose ONE Why run the app as a non-root user? A. Reduce impact if the app is compromised B. Make the image larger C. Skip tests D. Expose the database Answer: A. Explanation: Least privilege limits what a compromised process can change. Q8 - Choose ONE What does docker compose logs app show? A. Output from the app service B. Terraform state C. Git history D. Cloud billing only Answer: A. Explanation: Compose logs displays output emitted by the selected service. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which belong in .dockerignore? A. .env B. .git C. local node modules D. public README Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Excluding local secrets, Git metadata, and installed modules reduces risk and build context. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are good database container practices? A. Keep DB on private Compose network B. Use a named data volume C. Publish its port to everyone by default D. Add readiness health checking Answers: A, B, D. Explanation: Private access, persistence, and readiness checks improve the lab; public DB exposure is unsafe. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply What helps investigate an exiting container? A. docker compose logs B. docker compose ps -a C. docker inspect D. Delete volumes immediately Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Logs, state, and inspection provide evidence; deleting volumes risks data loss. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply Which are unsafe? A. Baking .env into the image B. Running as root without need C. Using privileged: true as a shortcut D. Reviewing Compose config Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: These increase credential exposure or container privileges; review is good practice. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 8 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 8 Troubleshooting
text: Week 8 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Next step --- --- --- Docker daemon unavailable Engine is stopped or Codespace lacks Docker access Run docker version; start Docker Desktop/Engine or use a supported host. Do not expose the socket publicly. npm ci fails Missing or mismatched package-lock.json Run npm install in the project, review the lockfile change, commit it, then rebuild. Container exits immediately Startup command failed or app listened on the wrong interface/port Run docker compose logs app; confirm app listens on 0.0.0.0, not only 127.0.0.1. App cannot resolve db Wrong Compose service name or services not on same network Check docker compose ps and docker compose config; use the service name as hostname. Database connection refused at startup Database is not ready Use a health check and depends on condition; app should retry transient startup failures. port is already allocated Host port already used Identify the listener; change only the host side of the mapping, e.g. "3001:3000". Data disappeared A volume was removed or a different project/volume was used Inspect docker volume ls and Compose project name; do not prune volumes. Secret appears in image .env was in build context or copied Stop sharing the image, rotate the secret, add .env to .dockerignore, rebuild. Useful checks: docker compose ps -a, docker compose logs app, docker inspect CONTAINER, docker compose config. Inspect output before sharing; it may include environment values.

title: Week 9: AWS Cloud Foundations
text: Week 9: AWS Cloud Foundations Project: CoraxReads Goal: Understand cloud identity, networking, billing, and a small compute deployment without treating cloud as free or risk-free. What you will ship - A cost budget and notification configured before resources. - A documented, small EC2 lab deployment reachable only through the ports you intend. - A teardown checklist with evidence that resources were removed. Three classes 1. Cloud accounts, IAM, and cost controls. 2. VPC, security groups, and EC2 networking. 3. Deploy, observe, and clean up a practice web service. Important cost and access rules - AWS usage can incur charges. Free-tier eligibility and prices vary by account, date, and region. - A budget alert is a warning, not a guaranteed spending cap; notifications can be delayed. - Enable MFA for the account owner. Do not use root credentials for daily work. - Use one AWS account for the course. Never put access keys or private SSH keys in Git. - Do not create resources until the instructor confirms your budget and cleanup plan. Lessons - Class 1: Account, identity, and budget - Class 2: Network and compute - Class 3: Deploy and tear down - Assignment 9 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 9 Official reference - AWS Well-Architected Framework - AWS Budgets

title: Assignment 9: Deploy a Small AWS Practice Site
text: Assignment 9: Deploy a Small AWS Practice Site Time: 3-4 hours, with instructor review before launch Never begin resource creation without an approved cost and teardown plan. Task 1 - Set the guardrails Enable MFA for the account owner, use an approved non-root identity, select the course region, create a cost budget with an email alert, and record your cleanup checklist. Ask the instructor to review before moving on. Task 2 - Plan the network access Write down the exact inbound ports and source ranges. Limit SSH to your current IP or use Session Manager. If the site must be publicly visible, expose HTTP only for the exercise. Keep database/admin ports private. Task 3 - Launch and connect Use an approved small instance type and Linux image. Add a purpose tag. Record the instance name and region in private notes. Connect using the approved method; if using SSH, keep the private key outside Git and set mode 400. Task 4 - Deploy and verify Install Nginx using the Class 3 commands. Check service status and run curl --fail http://localhost. If approved, open the site using its public address. Capture a sanitized screenshot. Task 5 - Inspect and clean up Record which security-group rule allowed the request. Stop and terminate resources as instructed. Check for leftover volumes, snapshots, load balancers, and public IP allocations. Include a checklist with each resource and its final state. Submit Architecture diagram, sanitized security-group summary, budget-alert proof with personal information hidden, deployment verification, cost notes, teardown checklist, and troubleshooting reflection. Never submit keys, tokens, account credentials, or public screenshots of sensitive account details.

title: Class 1: Account, Identity, and Budget
text: Class 1: Account, Identity, and Budget Time: 2 hours Run commands in: AWS Console for account setup; no compute resources yet. Cloud is someone else's computer, with your bill AWS provides services on demand. You still choose identity permissions, network access, and which resources run. The account owner is like the person who holds the building's master key; use a separate, least-privilege identity for normal work. Before creating compute 1. Sign in to the AWS account owner/root only for account-level tasks. 2. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root user. 3. Do not create root access keys. 4. Use IAM Identity Center or an instructor-approved IAM identity for regular work. 5. Select the course region and record it in your private lab notes. 6. In Billing and Cost Management, create a monthly cost budget and email alert at a small amount chosen with the instructor. 7. Verify the alert recipient and note that alerts may be delayed and do not stop resources. Do not post account IDs, billing screenshots with personal details, or credentials in a public portfolio. Practice without spending Use the console to inspect IAM, VPC, and EC2 pages without pressing Launch . Identify: - Who you are signed in as. - Which region is selected. - Which permissions the identity has. - Where to find budgets and cost reports. Ask for approval before any action that creates a paid resource.

title: Class 2: Network and Compute
text: Class 2: Network and Compute Time: 2 hours Tools: AWS Console. Create resources only after budget and instructor approval. Network: the building and its doors A VPC is your private network space. A subnet is a smaller network segment. A route table decides where traffic can go. A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface. For a beginner lab, use the account's default VPC only if the instructor confirms it is suitable. Do not change shared VPC settings. Security group rules Use only the inbound traffic your exercise needs: - HTTP TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 only when intentionally showing a public practice page. - SSH TCP 22 only from your current public IP, never from 0.0.0.0/0. - Do not open database ports publicly. An EC2 instance is a virtual computer. Its public IPv4 address may change after stop/start unless a paid static address is allocated; avoid allocating one for this lab. Select compute carefully Choose an instructor-approved, smallest suitable instance type and a supported Linux image. Pricing and free eligibility change; read the current estimate in the console before launch. Tag resources with an owner and purpose, for example Project=CoraxReadsLab. Do not create a Kubernetes cluster in this week. Managed clusters have additional costs.

title: Class 3: Deploy, Observe, and Tear Down
text: Class 3: Deploy, Observe, and Tear Down Time: 2 hours Tools: AWS Console and an SSH client or instructor-approved connection method. Connect without exposing credentials Use Session Manager or browser-based EC2 Instance Connect if enabled. If the lab uses SSH: 1. Store the downloaded private key outside your repository. 2. Restrict its file permission with chmod 400 path/to/key.pem. 3. Confirm the security group allows port 22 only from your current IP. 4. Use the correct image username (for Ubuntu images this is commonly ubuntu). 5. Never share the private key or paste it into a chat. chmod 400 makes the key readable only by its owner. SSH rejects keys with overly broad permissions. Install and serve a practice page On the approved Ubuntu instance: - apt update refreshes package metadata. - apt install installs Nginx. - systemctl enable --now starts the service now and at boot. - status checks the service state. - tee writes the simple practice page with administrator permission. - chmod 644 gives the web server read access without making the page executable. - curl checks the local HTTP response. Use the public address in a browser only if port 80 is intentionally open. Never open an admin or database port to the internet. Teardown is part of the lab 1. Save evidence without exposing keys, account IDs, or private information. 2. Stop and then terminate the EC2 instance when instructed. 3. Check for unattached EBS volumes, snapshots, load balancers, public IP allocations, and other resources. 4. Confirm the instance is terminated and no lab resources remain. 5. Review the billing dashboard later; charges can post after resource deletion.

title: Quiz Week 9: AWS Cloud Foundations
text: Quiz Week 9: AWS Cloud Foundations 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does an AWS budget alert do? A. Warns about estimated/actual spend; it is not a guaranteed cap B. Automatically prevents all charges C. Deletes resources D. Replaces MFA Answer: A. Explanation: Budgets notify; they do not reliably stop all usage. Q2 - Choose ONE Which identity should not be used for daily work? A. Root account owner B. Instructor-approved least-privilege identity C. A role for one task D. Federated course identity Answer: A. Explanation: Root has broad account authority and should be reserved for account-level tasks. Q3 - Choose ONE What does MFA add? A. A second proof of identity B. A public IP C. More disk space D. A Git commit Answer: A. Explanation: MFA requires an additional authentication factor. Q4 - Choose ONE What is a security group? A. A stateful network firewall for a resource B. A book catalog C. A file archive D. An SSH private key Answer: A. Explanation: Security groups control allowed inbound and outbound traffic. Q5 - Choose ONE What is a safer SSH rule for a practice VM? A. Port 22 only from your current IP B. All ports from everywhere C. Database port from everywhere D. No rule review Answer: A. Explanation: Narrow source ranges reduce exposure. Q6 - Choose ONE What does chmod 400 key.pem do? A. Makes the key owner-readable only B. Makes it public C. Deletes the key D. Starts SSH Answer: A. Explanation: Mode 400 restricts read access to the owner. Q7 - Choose ONE What should happen before launching a resource? A. Review cost, region, permissions, and cleanup plan B. Assume free tier means free C. Disable MFA D. Open every inbound port Answer: A. Explanation: Resource creation can incur cost and exposure, so plan first. Q8 - Choose ONE What happens to an instance's public IPv4 after stop/start? A. It may change B. It becomes a database password C. It is always permanent D. It is deleted from Git Answer: A. Explanation: A dynamically assigned address may change; static allocation can add cost. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply What should be checked during cleanup? A. EC2 instances B. Unattached volumes and snapshots C. Load balancers and public IP allocations D. Only the browser tab Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Related resources can continue to incur cost after the VM is gone. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which are good account practices? A. Enable root MFA B. Avoid root access keys C. Use least privilege for routine work D. Commit keys to a private repo Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: MFA and least privilege reduce risk; private repos do not make secrets safe. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which ports should not be exposed publicly by default? A. PostgreSQL database port B. Administrative interfaces C. SSH from every IP D. HTTP when intentionally serving a public page Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Databases/admin interfaces and unrestricted SSH should remain private; HTTP may be intentionally public. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply What is true about free-tier pricing? A. Eligibility and limits can change B. A budget alert is not a hard cap C. Resources can incur charges outside eligible limits D. All AWS services are always free Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Free-tier limits vary, alerts are delayed/not a stop control, and many services cost money. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 9 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 9 Troubleshooting
text: Week 9 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- SSH times out Wrong address, no route, or port 22 not allowed from your IP Confirm instance state/address/region; check the security-group source range. Do not open SSH to the whole internet. SSH says key permissions are too open Private key file is readable by others Use chmod 400 KEYFILE; keep the key outside Git. SSH permission denied Wrong username/key/identity or key pair Confirm image username and selected key. Do not share the private key to debug. Website times out Nginx stopped or port 80 not allowed Check service locally with systemctl status nginx; inspect the security group only for intended HTTP access. Website returns 403/404 Wrong web-root content or permissions Check Nginx logs and /var/www/html; grant read access without making files world-writable. Budget email did not arrive Alert threshold, recipient verification, or reporting delay Verify budget configuration and email; remember a budget is not a hard cap. Unexpected charge appears Resource remains or delayed billing report Inspect the regional resource inventory and billing details; terminate approved lab resources and notify the instructor. Never solve connectivity by opening all ports to 0.0.0.0/0. Stop and ask for review if you cannot identify a resource or its cost.

title: Week 10: Kubernetes Fundamentals
text: Week 10: Kubernetes Fundamentals Project: CoraxReads Goal: Run a small application on local Kubernetes and understand how desired state, networking, and health checks fit together. What you will ship - A local kind cluster. - A namespace, Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap. - A runbook for checking pods, logs, and rollout status. Three classes 1. Cluster objects: Pods, Deployments, labels, and namespaces. 2. Networking and configuration: Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and port-forwarding. 3. Reliability: probes, resource requests, rollout, rollback, and cleanup. This week uses a local cluster. A local kind cluster avoids managed-cluster costs. Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded by default, not automatically encrypted. Lessons - Class 1: Run a workload - Class 2: Expose and configure it - Class 3: Health, rollout, and cleanup - Assignment 10 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 10 Official reference - Kubernetes concepts - kind documentation

title: Assignment 10: Run CoraxReads on Local Kubernetes
text: Assignment 10: Run CoraxReads on Local Kubernetes Time: 3-4 hours Submit in: your portfolio repository. Do not create a paid managed cluster for this assignment. Task 1 - Create and check the cluster Start Docker, create a kind cluster named coraxreads, then run kubectl get nodes. Save the output and explain what Ready means. Task 2 - Create desired-state files Write YAML for a Deployment with two replicas and a Service selecting its Pods. Use consistent labels. Run kubectl apply -f on the files. Task 3 - Inspect and expose locally Run kubectl get deployments,pods,services,endpoints, then kubectl describe the Deployment. Start port-forwarding and verify with curl --fail http://localhost:8080. Task 4 - Add reliability Add readiness/liveness probes and resource requests/limits. Apply changes and run kubectl rollout status. Change the image to a deliberately invalid tag in the lab, inspect the rollout failure and events, restore the valid image, apply, and verify recovery. Task 5 - Explain and clean up Submit an architecture diagram, YAML, command explanations, sanitized output for success and failure, and a cleanup checklist. Remove only your named resources and local kind cluster. Pass checklist - Service endpoints select the expected Pods. - Health checks pass. - The bad image is diagnosed and corrected. - No plaintext credentials are committed. - Cleanup is verified.

title: Class 1: Run a Workload
text: Class 1: Run a Workload Time: 2 hours Run commands in: a local kind cluster with Docker working. Objects as a restaurant A Pod is one running instance, like a kitchen station. A Deployment is the manager that keeps the requested number of stations available. A Service is a stable address that directs requests to matching Pods. Create a cluster: - kind create cluster runs Kubernetes nodes in local containers. - cluster-info shows API access. - get nodes confirms the cluster has a ready node. Apply a Deployment: Save as deployment.yaml, then run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. apply asks the API server to converge the live object toward the YAML's desired state. Check: get gives a summary; describe includes events and selector details.

title: Class 2: Expose and Configure It
text: Class 2: Expose and Configure It Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the local cluster. Stable in-cluster access Create service.yaml: The Service selector matches Pod labels. port is the Service port; targetPort is the container port. Apply and inspect: Keep the last command running; in another terminal open http://localhost:8080. port-forward creates a local tunnel; it does not make the app public. Non-secret configuration A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration. Never put passwords in a ConfigMap. A Kubernetes Secret is also not a secure vault by default; access is controlled by RBAC and encryption-at-rest configuration. For this lab, keep app settings in ConfigMaps and do not create real credentials. In production, use an approved secret manager and narrowly scoped service accounts. Practice Change the Deployment replica count from two to three. Apply it and watch kubectl get pods -w. Explain what changed and how the Service finds the new Pod.

title: Class 3: Health, Rollout, and Cleanup
text: Class 3: Health, Rollout, and Cleanup Time: 2 hours Run commands in: the local cluster. Add health and resource settings Add these fields to the container: - Requests help the scheduler find capacity. - Limits cap container resource use. - Readiness decides when a Pod receives traffic. - Liveness restarts a container that is stuck unhealthy. Use values appropriate to the app; these small values are only a lab example. Roll out and roll back rollout status waits for the update, history shows revisions, and undo returns to the previous revision. Verify after rollback. Logs and cleanup Logs explain container output. Delete commands remove the named lab objects; kind delete cluster removes the local cluster. Verify the cluster name before deleting.

title: Quiz Week 10: Kubernetes
text: Quiz Week 10: Kubernetes 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What does a Deployment maintain? A. Desired Pod replicas and rollout B. AWS billing C. Git commits D. DNS registration Answer: A. Explanation: A Deployment manages replica sets and converges Pods toward desired state. Q2 - Choose ONE What does a Service provide? A. Stable access to matching Pods B. A container image build C. A private SSH key D. A Docker volume Answer: A. Explanation: A Service selects Pods and provides a stable network endpoint. Q3 - Choose ONE What does a readiness probe control? A. Whether a Pod should receive traffic B. How Git tags are named C. Cloud region selection D. Docker image layers Answer: A. Explanation: Readiness indicates whether the app is ready to serve requests. Q4 - Choose ONE What is kubectl port-forward for? A. A local tunnel to a Kubernetes resource B. Publicly opening every node port C. Creating an AWS VPC D. Saving a database backup Answer: A. Explanation: Port-forward creates a local connection to a selected resource. Q5 - Choose ONE What does kubectl rollout status do? A. Waits for rollout progress and reports status B. Deletes old Git branches C. Exposes a secret D. Rebuilds the image Answer: A. Explanation: It reports whether the Deployment rollout completes. Q6 - Choose ONE What do resource requests help Kubernetes do? A. Schedule Pods based on needed capacity B. Encrypt environment variables automatically C. Create DNS records D. Write application code Answer: A. Explanation: Requests inform scheduling and resource placement. Q7 - Choose ONE What does a ConfigMap hold? A. Non-sensitive configuration B. Automatically encrypted credentials C. Docker image layers D. Git history Answer: A. Explanation: ConfigMaps are for non-secret configuration; they are not secret stores. Q8 - Choose ONE What is the security status of base64 Kubernetes Secret data? A. Encoded, not automatically encrypted B. Publicly invisible forever C. A password hash D. Encrypted by definition Answer: A. Explanation: Base64 is reversible encoding; use RBAC and approved encryption/secret management. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply Which commands help diagnose a Pod? A. kubectl describe pod B. kubectl logs C. kubectl get events D. git tag Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Describe, logs, and events show state and failure evidence. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply What should match for a Service to route to Pods? A. Service selector labels B. Pod labels C. The app port/target port D. The Git commit message Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Selectors identify Pods and ports determine traffic destination. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply What is useful for production workloads? A. Readiness probe B. Appropriate resource requests C. Least-privilege service account D. Run every container as privileged Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Health, capacity planning, and least privilege improve operations; privileged mode expands risk. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply What should be verified before deleting a cluster? A. Current kubectl context B. Cluster name C. That the cluster is the disposable lab D. Nothing; delete all contexts Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Confirm context and target so shared or production resources are not removed. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 10 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 10 Troubleshooting
text: Week 10 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- kubectl cannot connect Cluster is stopped or wrong context selected Run kubectl config current-context and kind get clusters; select only the intended local context. Pod is ImagePullBackOff Image/tag unavailable or registry blocked Run kubectl describe pod; check Events and image spelling. Pod is CrashLoopBackOff Process exits repeatedly Run kubectl logs POD --previous and inspect startup configuration. Service has no endpoints Selector does not match Pod labels or Pods are not Ready Compare Service selector with Pod labels; inspect readiness probe and Pod status. Port-forward connection refused Wrong service/port or no ready endpoint Check kubectl get svc,endpoints,pods; use matching service and target port. kubectl apply rejects YAML Indentation/schema/field issue Read the exact line and resource kind; check API structure and reapply. Pod never Ready Probe path/port wrong or app not listening Inspect logs and events; verify the app binds to the expected container port. kubectl describe and Events are often the fastest first evidence. Do not delete the whole cluster to fix a single object until you have captured diagnostics.

title: Week 11: CI/CD and Observability
text: Week 11: CI/CD and Observability Project: CoraxReads Goal: Automatically test changes, build a versioned container, and use signals to tell whether a release is healthy. The course repository includes a working CoraxReads CI workflow that students can inspect and adapt. What you will ship - A pull-request workflow that runs tests and builds the app image. - A documented deployment approval and rollback process. - A small monitoring dashboard with an actionable alert. Three classes 1. Continuous integration: workflow triggers, checks, artifacts, and status. 2. Continuous delivery: image tags, environments, approvals, and rollback. 3. Observability: logs, metrics, dashboards, alerts, and incident notes. CI checks whether a change is safe to merge. CD delivers a reviewed change. Observability explains how the running system behaves. Safety rules - Start with pull-request tests; do not auto-deploy every branch. - Use least-privilege identity and short-lived credentials such as OIDC where supported. - Require approval for production deployment. - Never print secrets into workflow logs. - Do not enable a public dashboard without authentication and network restrictions. Lessons - Class 1: CI workflow - Class 2: Delivery and rollback - Class 3: Metrics, logs, and alerts - Assignment 11 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 11 Official reference - GitHub Actions documentation - Prometheus documentation - Grafana documentation

title: Assignment 11: CI, Delivery, and Service Health
text: Assignment 11: CI, Delivery, and Service Health Time: 3-4 hours Submit in: your portfolio repository and approved practice environment. Task 1 - Add CI Create a GitHub Actions workflow for pull requests and pushes to the default branch. Run locked dependency installation, automated tests, and an image build. Give the workflow read-only permissions unless a specific job needs more. Task 2 - Prove it works Open a pull request and capture a passing run. Then make a harmless test failure in a temporary branch, observe the red check, fix it, and verify green. Do not merge a failing change. Task 3 - Design safe delivery Draw the path from merge to test deployment. State the artifact identifier, who approves production, which identity deploys, and how the previous version is restored. Do not add a cloud secret to the workflow. Task 4 - Build an observability view Choose three signals: availability, error rate, and latency are a good start. Build a local or clearly labeled sample dashboard. Add a runbook link and one alert condition with a duration and owner. Task 5 - Test the response Trigger a safe local failure, find its log, observe the health signal, and write the response steps. Restore the service and record recovery evidence. Submit Workflow file, sanitized run link, delivery diagram, dashboard screenshot, alert/runbook, failure and recovery notes, and security review. Do not submit tokens or logs containing sensitive data.

title: Class 1: Continuous Integration
text: Class 1: Continuous Integration Time: 2 hours Run commands in: your portfolio repository; workflow examples belong in .github/workflows/. Pipeline as an automated teammate A starter Node workflow: - on declares events that start the workflow. - permissions grants only read access needed for checkout. - npm ci installs locked dependencies reproducibly. - npm test runs the project checks. - docker build confirms an image can be created. This starter uses major action tags for readability. In a real repository, pin third-party actions to reviewed full commit SHAs and update them deliberately. Add the workflow to your app/portfolio repository and open a PR. Read the run log from the first failed step; do not paste tokens or secrets into logs.

title: Class 2: Delivery and Rollback
text: Class 2: Delivery and Rollback Time: 2 hours Tools: GitHub Actions, a container registry, and an approved test environment. Build once, promote the same artifact Tag an image with an immutable identifier such as a commit SHA, not only latest. The image tested in CI should be the image promoted to the test environment. Separate checks from deployment - Pull request: tests, static checks, image build. - Merge to protected main: publish a versioned artifact. - Test environment: deploy and run a health check. - Production environment: require approval and use scoped identity. Do not grant pull-request jobs access to production credentials. Prefer OIDC federation to long-lived cloud access keys. Restrict the role trust policy to the expected repository, branch/environment, and audience. Release controls - Protect the default branch and require passing checks. - Store deploy permissions in a protected environment. - Keep secrets in the approved secret store, not in YAML. - Record image digest, deployment time, approver, and health result. - Roll back to the last known-good image and verify health. Practice Draw the pipeline and mark which steps can run for every pull request and which require approval. Explain what happens if the new image fails its health check.

title: Class 3: Metrics, Logs, and Alerts
text: Class 3: Metrics, Logs, and Alerts Time: 2 hours Tools: Your local lab app; Prometheus/Grafana may run locally in Docker. Three kinds of evidence - Metrics: numbers over time, such as request count or latency. - Logs: timestamped events that explain what a component did. - Traces: a request's path across components. Think of a shop: metrics say how many customers waited; logs record a specific order error; a trace follows one order from the counter to the stock room. Dashboard first Choose a question before adding a chart: - Is the service up? - Are errors increasing? - Is request latency getting worse? - Is the database reachable? A dashboard should answer operational questions, not just look busy. Label units, time range, and service. Alerts should lead to action An alert needs a condition, duration, severity, owner, and runbook. Alert on user impact (for example sustained failed health checks), not every small CPU change. Test the alert safely in a local lab. Never put credentials, personal information, or full request bodies in logs. Restrict dashboard access; dashboards can reveal operational details. Practice Trigger one known test failure. Find it in logs, identify a metric that would reveal impact, and write one actionable alert plus the first two runbook steps.

title: Quiz Week 11: CI/CD and Observability
text: Quiz Week 11: CI/CD and Observability 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What is the primary purpose of CI? A. Automatically validate proposed changes B. Replace all code review C. Store cloud passwords in YAML D. Delete failed branches Answer: A. Explanation: CI runs repeatable checks so teams have early feedback on changes. Q2 - Choose ONE Why use npm ci in CI? A. Reproducibly install from the lockfile B. Update all dependencies unpredictably C. Start a cloud VM D. Write the README Answer: A. Explanation: npm ci installs the locked dependency tree. Q3 - Choose ONE Why tag images with a commit SHA or digest? A. Identify the exact artifact B. Make it publicly accessible C. Remove need for testing D. Hide build logs Answer: A. Explanation: Immutable identifiers make it possible to know exactly what was tested and deployed. Q4 - Choose ONE Why should production deployment require approval? A. Add a deliberate control before a high-impact change B. Make CI slower for no reason C. Avoid health checks D. Share root credentials Answer: A. Explanation: Approval adds a human control for sensitive environments. Q5 - Choose ONE What does OIDC commonly provide in cloud deployment? A. Short-lived federated identity instead of a stored long-lived key B. A database schema C. A Grafana chart D. A container volume Answer: A. Explanation: Federation can exchange workflow identity for scoped temporary credentials. Q6 - Choose ONE What does a metric show? A. A numeric measurement over time B. A full application source file C. A Git conflict D. A secret password Answer: A. Explanation: Metrics are time-series measurements such as latency or request count. Q7 - Choose ONE What should a useful alert include? A. Condition, duration, severity, owner, and action B. A chart color only C. Every log line D. No runbook Answer: A. Explanation: An actionable alert tells someone why it fired and what to do. Q8 - Choose ONE Which workflow should not receive production credentials? A. Untrusted pull-request job B. Protected deployment environment C. Approved release job D. A narrowly scoped deploy role Answer: A. Explanation: Untrusted PR code could expose credentials, so it must not receive production access. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply What belongs in a CI pull-request job? A. Tests B. Static validation C. Image build D. Production root key Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: CI can validate and build; root keys do not belong in workflow jobs. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply Which practices reduce workflow risk? A. Minimal permissions B. Pin actions to reviewed commit SHAs C. Protect deployment environments D. Print secrets to logs Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Least privilege, pinning, and approvals reduce supply-chain and deployment risks. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which observability signals are useful? A. Metrics B. Logs C. Traces D. Unlabeled screenshots only Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: These signals provide quantitative, event, and request-flow evidence. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply What helps with a failed release? A. Roll back to a known-good artifact B. Check health after rollback C. Record which artifact was deployed D. Delete all logs Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Known-good rollback, verification, and artifact traceability support recovery. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 11 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 11 Troubleshooting
text: Week 11 Troubleshooting Problem Likely reason Safe next step --- --- --- Workflow does not start Trigger/branch name mismatch or workflow file path wrong Check .github/workflows, event type, default branch, and Actions settings. npm ci fails Lockfile is missing or out of sync Run install locally, review and commit the lockfile, then retry. Docker build works locally but not CI Missing file in context, platform difference, or unpinned dependency Inspect build logs and .dockerignore; reproduce from a clean checkout. Secret is empty in a job Secret not configured for repository/environment or job lacks permission Verify protected secret scope and environment approval; never print it for debugging. Deploy job runs on untrusted PR Workflow permissions/conditions are too broad Remove deployment credentials from PR jobs; restrict deployment to protected branches/environments. Dashboard has no data Exporter not running or scrape target wrong Inspect Prometheus targets and service networking; verify /metrics from the monitor container. Alert fires constantly Threshold/window or query is wrong Validate the query against a test signal, set a sensible duration, and document the expected action. Alert is ignored No owner or useful runbook Assign an owner, reduce noise, and include exact first checks in the runbook. When an action fails, read the first failing step and relevant lines of log. Redact credentials and personally identifiable information before sharing output.

title: Week 12: CoraxReads Capstone
text: Week 12: CoraxReads Capstone Goal: Demonstrate the full path from a code change to a secure, observable, recoverable service. Your final story Show how a browser request reaches CoraxReads, how your code is tested, how the app is packaged and deployed, how you know it is healthy, and how you recover if it is not.
