Required portfolio pieces - Architecture diagram and README. - Application and database run instructions. - Infrastructure/configuration artifacts used in your project. - CI run and deployment evidence. - Monitoring dashboard, alert, and runbook. - Security and cost checklist. - Demo and reflection. Three classes 1. Assemble: architecture, deployment path, and operational documentation. 2. Rehearse: failure injection, incident communication, recovery, and cost cleanup. 3. Present: demo, peer review, and next-step plan. Lessons - Class 1: Assemble the evidence - Class 2: Rehearse an incident - Class 3: Demo and reflect - Assignment 12 - Troubleshooting - Quiz Week 12 Official reference - Google SRE book: monitoring distributed systems - NIST incident response recommendations

title: Assignment 12: Present the CoraxReads Capstone
text: Assignment 12: Present the CoraxReads Capstone Time: 4-6 hours Submit in: your portfolio repository. Task 1 - Finish the architecture and README Update the architecture diagram to match the real implementation. Write the README using the Class 1 order. Test each command from a fresh checkout or have a peer follow it. Task 2 - Show the delivery path Link a reviewed pull request, passing CI run, image identifier, and deployment evidence. Explain where approval happens and what identity is used. Redact sensitive details. Task 3 - Show operations Provide a dashboard with at least three useful signals, one actionable alert, and a runbook. Show a sanitized successful health check. Task 4 - Rehearse recovery In a disposable environment, trigger one safe failure. Capture the timeline, evidence, recovery action, and verification. Restore the environment and prove it is healthy again. Task 5 - Close the account footprint Check and clean up all lab compute, disks, snapshots, IP allocations, load balancers, clusters, containers, and other billable resources. Never delete shared or production resources. Record final checks without exposing account identifiers. Task 6 - Present and reflect Give a five-minute demo. Include one thing that broke, one design tradeoff, and one next improvement. Ask for peer review and update your README. Evaluation rubric (100 points) - Working system and reproducible setup: 20 - Architecture and documentation: 15 - Tests and CI: 15 - Secure identity, secrets, and network choices: 15 - Monitoring, alert, and runbook: 15 - Recovery and cost cleanup: 10 - Clear demo and honest reflection: 10 Pass the course badge only after required sections are complete and reviewed.

title: Class 1: Assemble the Evidence
text: Class 1: Assemble the Evidence Time: 2 hours Tools: your portfolio repository and project environment. One diagram, one source of truth Draw the actual system, not the system you hoped to build. Include: - Browser/user entry point. - App and database. - Network boundaries and allowed ports. - CI workflow and deployment environment. - Monitoring, logs, and backup location. Use arrows to show traffic and label external dependencies. Never put credentials or sensitive addresses in the diagram. README order 1. What CoraxReads does. 2. Architecture picture. 3. Prerequisites and supported versions. 4. Local start and stop steps. 5. Test commands and expected results. 6. Deployment and rollback. 7. Monitoring and troubleshooting. 8. Cost and cleanup. 9. Known limitations and next improvements. Every command should say where to run it and what success looks like. Test the instructions from a clean checkout if possible. Evidence Use links to pull requests, CI runs, and sanitized screenshots. Explain what each screenshot proves. A screenshot is not a substitute for reproducible configuration.

title: Class 2: Rehearse an Incident
text: Class 2: Rehearse an Incident Time: 2 hours Rule: Rehearse only in a local/disposable environment you own. Incident scenario The app's health endpoint returns an error after a deployment. You are on call. Use this order: 1. Protect users: decide whether to pause rollout or roll back. 2. Observe: inspect health, recent deployment, metrics, and logs. 3. Hypothesize: state one likely cause and evidence for it. 4. Recover: use a reviewed rollback or fix in the lab. 5. Verify: check health and a user-facing request. 6. Learn: write a short timeline and one prevention action. Communication template Keep communication factual. Do not blame a person. Do not include passwords, tokens, customer data, or sensitive account details. Cost cleanup drill List every resource you created in the course, identify its owner/environment, and check its final state. A stopped resource may still cost money (for example storage). Verify each service's resource inventory and billing, not only the VM state.

title: Class 3: Demo and Reflect
text: Class 3: Demo and Reflect Time: 2 hours Audience: a technical peer and a non-technical stakeholder. Five-minute demo 1. Problem: Who needs the bookstore and why? 2. Architecture: Explain the request path using your diagram. 3. Change: Show a small reviewed feature and passing CI. 4. Operations: Show a health check and one useful dashboard/alert. 5. Recovery: Explain the rollback and demonstrate it in the lab if safe. 6. Learning: Name a failure, how you diagnosed it, and what you changed. Avoid saying "it is secure" or "it scales" without evidence. State limitations and what you would improve next. Peer review Ask your reviewer to check whether they can: - Start the system using only the README. - Identify where secrets belong and where they must not go. - Find the latest passing build and deployment evidence. - Follow the first steps in your runbook. Finish Confirm cloud resources are cleaned up, secrets are absent from Git, and the portfolio links work. Add the earned badge only after the weekly assessment passes.

title: Quiz Week 12: Capstone Operations
text: Quiz Week 12: Capstone Operations 12 questions, 20 minutes. 8 Choose ONE, 4 Choose ALL that apply. Pass: 11 out of 12. Questions Q1 - Choose ONE What should an architecture diagram show? A. The actual components and their request paths B. Only a decorative logo C. Credentials D. Every learner's personal data Answer: A. Explanation: A useful diagram describes real components and how traffic moves. Q2 - Choose ONE What proves a README is usable? A. A peer can follow it from a clean checkout B. It has many pages C. It says "works on my machine" D. It omits prerequisites Answer: A. Explanation: A clean reproduction tests whether instructions are complete. Q3 - Choose ONE What is the first goal during a service incident? A. Protect users and assess impact B. Find someone to blame C. Delete logs D. Hide the alert Answer: A. Explanation: Incident response prioritizes safety and user impact. Q4 - Choose ONE Why verify health after rollback? A. Confirm recovery actually worked B. Make the dashboard colorful C. Avoid checking logs D. Change Git history Answer: A. Explanation: A rollback command is not proof that the service recovered. Q5 - Choose ONE What belongs in an incident update? A. Impact, evidence, action, and current status B. Passwords and tokens C. Blame D. Unverified guesses as facts Answer: A. Explanation: Factual updates help stakeholders understand status without exposing secrets. Q6 - Choose ONE Why preserve immutable image identifiers? A. Know exactly what was tested and deployed B. Make every image public C. Replace source control D. Hide the build time Answer: A. Explanation: Immutable identifiers provide artifact traceability. Q7 - Choose ONE What is a budget alert? A. A notification, not a guaranteed spending cap B. An automatic deletion policy C. A free-tier promise D. An SSH key Answer: A. Explanation: Alerts can arrive late and do not necessarily stop resource usage. Q8 - Choose ONE What is a good portfolio demo? A. Show evidence, explain tradeoffs, and state limitations B. Claim zero risk C. Hide all failures D. Show credentials to prove access Answer: A. Explanation: Honest evidence and limitations show engineering judgment. Q9 - Choose ALL that apply What belongs in a capstone README? A. Prerequisites and startup steps B. Tests and expected results C. Monitoring and recovery notes D. Real passwords Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Reproducible instructions, validation, and operations help users; secrets must not be published. Q10 - Choose ALL that apply What should be checked during cloud cleanup? A. Compute instances B. Storage and snapshots C. Public IP allocations/load balancers D. Only the local browser Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Many related resources can incur charges after compute stops. Q11 - Choose ALL that apply Which are good incident practices? A. Capture a timeline B. Preserve useful sanitized evidence C. Verify service after recovery D. Delete logs before review Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Timeline, evidence, and verification support recovery and learning. Q12 - Choose ALL that apply What makes a runbook useful? A. Clear first checks B. Exact safe recovery steps C. Owner and escalation path D. Unexplained destructive commands Answers: A, B, C. Explanation: Runbooks should be actionable, owned, and safe; unexplained deletion is dangerous. Scoring 11 to 12: Pass, earn Week 12 badge. Below 11: review the explanations and retake once.

title: Week 12 Troubleshooting
text: Week 12 Troubleshooting Problem What to check Next step --- --- --- Reviewer cannot start the app Missing prerequisite, environment variable, or startup command Test from a clean checkout; list exact versions and provide .env.example with placeholders. Diagram does not match implementation It describes a planned rather than current system Update it to the deployed components and label planned items as planned. CI evidence is missing Wrong branch/run link or retention/access issue Link the workflow run and explain which job validates each property. Dashboard has no useful signal It shows infrastructure noise without user impact Start from availability, error rate, latency, and data-store health. Rollback is not possible Artifact or previous config was not retained Preserve immutable artifacts and document restore steps before deployment. Cloud bill continues after VM stop Disks, snapshots, addresses, or other resources remain Inventory by region and resource type; remove only identified lab resources. Demo fails live Network or external dependency is unavailable Have sanitized screenshots/log evidence and describe the failure truthfully; do not claim success without proof. If cleanup could affect a shared account or another learner, stop and ask the account owner before deleting anything.
